title: The datasets
text:
What this page is for: here, for each data file, is where it comes from and exactly what each column means — with the unit alongside, what is in it, and how much is missing. Not a lesson — a reference. It sits at the back because you don’t have to read it beforehand; you open it the moment you think, in the middle of an exercise: hang on, what is that, actually? From every exercise an arrow points here, in the data strip at the top.
These are the files the exercises use. To look one up: the table of contents alongside names each file, and every column is written exactly as it is in the file — so searching for bill_depth_mm works.
In every table, what is in it gives the lowest and the highest number that occurs, or for a word column every value with how often it occurs — so Adelie (151) means: the word Adelie, 151 times. Missing counts the empty spots. Those numbers come from the files themselves: they are read from them when the Dutch original of this page is built, and this English page is checked against that original number by number — so if it ever says 342 when the file has long said something else, the check says so. What was written by hand is the meaning — that a column is called bill_depth_mm, the data tells you; that it is the height of the bill and not the width, someone has to tell you.

title: The datasets
section: stones.csv — the twelve stones from the book
text:
stones.csv — the twelve stones from the book
⬇ Download — stones.csv
These twelve are ours. They come not from an archive but from the book itself: Anna through to Leen are the stones with which the book tells the whole story, from the mean in chapter 1 to the crow in chapter 12. So few rows that you take them in at a glance, with just enough columns to practise everything on — and small enough to check every number by hand if you don’t believe it.
One thing was deliberately adjusted, and you ought to know it in case you ever come across an older printout: on 9 August 2026, 0.6 carat was added to every stone. Before that the mean was exactly 1.00, and now it is 1.60.

Why that was done — you can safely skip this until you reach chapter 4. Further on you learn centring: taking the mean off every value, so that zero comes to lie on the mean. With a mean of exactly 1.00 that is the same as subtracting 1, and then you can’t see what is actually happening. There is a second gain too. The regression line has a starting point: what it predicts at zero carats. With these numbers that is a negative shine — and a stone of zero carats does not exist, so that starting point means nothing. Not an address where nobody lives, but an address that does not exist. Exactly the reason to centre, and much easier to explain when you see it happen. Such a shift, by the way, touches only that starting point: the slope, r, R² and p stay exactly the same.

title: The datasets
text:
penguins.csv — penguins off Antarctica
⬇ Download — penguins.csv
Between 2007 and 2009 the biologist Kristen Gorman and her colleagues walked three small islands of the Palmer archipelago, right by the American research station in Antarctica. They were looking for nests of three penguin species — Adélie, Gentoo and Chinstrap (the one with the thin black line under its chin, hence the name) — and for every animal they could get hold of they noted down the bill, the flipper and the weight. The question behind that work had nothing to do with us: they wanted to know how males and females of the same species differ in size, and how that ties in with what there is to eat in the sea.
This is real fieldwork, and it shows. The source counts 344 animals; for two of them one of the measurements failed, and we left those out. For nine of the remaining animals the sex was never established — they are in, with NA in that spot. The measurements are freely available (CC0).
For most of the animals the researchers also took a little blood, at the start of the breeding season. A lab read from it what the animal had eaten in the weeks before. Those are the last two columns, nitrogen and carbon.
Careful, because the names wrong-foot you: there is no amount of nitrogen or carbon in there. Every number is a difference from a fixed reference point that is set at zero. On nitrogen all the penguins sit above it, on carbon all of them below — which is why that column is negative. What they say is about the food:

nitrogen — what the animal ate. The higher the number, the more fish and the less krill (the tiny shrimps at the bottom of the food chain).
carbon — where the animal looked for its food. Which way means what, we leave aside here; use it to compare groups, not to interpret a single animal.

One number on its own says little; it comes alive when you lay groups side by side. The mean of nitrogen per species: Adelie 8.86, Gentoo 8.25, Chinstrap 9.36. Chinstrap sits highest: that species ate, on average, a little more fish in those weeks than the other two.
For twelve animals a result is missing. In that spot it says NA, and that can happen in two ways:

eleven animals are missing both columns: nine times there was too little blood, twice no blood was taken;
one animal is missing only nitrogen: the result never came back from the lab.

That is not an error in the file but a gap from the field, and it has a consequence. Compute with nitrogen, and those animals cannot take part: you compute with 330 penguins instead of 342; with carbon with 331, and with both at once also with 330 — not fewer, because whoever is missing carbon is missing nitrogen too. So look first at how many are missing, and write down how many animals you computed with.

section: airquality.csv — a summer over New York
text:
airquality.csv — a summer over New York
⬇ Download — airquality.csv
From 1 May to 30 September 1973, measurements were taken over New York every day. The ozone comes from the New York State Department of Conservation, which measured on Roosevelt Island between one and three in the afternoon; the weather data come from the National Weather Service. And mind: each number comes from a different spot in the city. The sun was measured in Central Park, the wind and the temperature at LaGuardia airport. That is not sloppiness but the usual way of things with air measurements — and it is at once a good reason to be careful with “the temperature that day”.
Ozone at street level is the stuff smog is made of, and it forms when sunlight acts on exhaust fumes — so you expect more ozone on warm, sunny, windless days. The source counts 153 days; on some of them the ozone measurement failed. We kept the days on which it did work — and even within those days the solar radiation is still missing five times. That comes with it: a series of measurements with gaps is the normal state, not an error.

title: The datasets
text:
bigfive.csv — 25 questions about yourself
⬇ Download — bigfive.csv
From a large online personality study that the psychologist William Revelle ran from 2010 (the SAPA project). Participants were shown statements about themselves and said, for each statement, how well it fitted them, on a scale from 1 (very inaccurate) to 6 (very accurate). The statements themselves come from the International Personality Item Pool, a freely usable collection of personality questions.
Two words from the source description to carry with you: self-report and online. Nobody spoke to these people, measured them or checked up on them. They landed on a website, filled in what they thought of themselves, and left again. Whoever took part picked themselves; what is there is what someone wrote down about themselves. That is no reason to put the file away — it is how a large part of personality research gets its data — but it is the reason there are things in it that cannot be. One of them is below, and that one is worth keeping.
The source has 25 statements and 2800 people, and those 25 belong to five traits of five statements each: agreeableness (A1–A5), conscientiousness (C1–C5), extraversion (E1–E5), neuroticism (N1–N5) and openness (O1–O5). All 25 are in here, with age, sex and level of education alongside.
We keep 2634 of the 2800 people: everyone who answered all ten neuroticism and openness statements. That is a choice from an earlier version of this file, left in on purpose, so that the exercises that already count on it keep their numbers.
So on the other columns an answer is missing here and there — exactly how many is in the column missing below, per column. When you work out a trait, let those people drop out. So rowMeans(...) and not rowMeans(..., na.rm = TRUE): the latter averages over whichever questions someone happened to fill in, so that whoever answered one of the five gets a scale score made from one question — and in the column it looks exactly like all the others.
Seven of the 25 statements are reversed. “Don’t talk a lot” belongs to extraversion, but whoever agrees with that sentence is in fact less extraverted. In the table below every such item carries a warning. Average the five statements of a trait without reversing them first, and you add two directions together and measure something other than you think — how hard that hits, you see in the exercise on Cronbach’s alpha (in Dutch). The neuroticism statements are the only five that all point the same way.
You reverse by subtracting the score from 7 — the two ends of the scale added together. Whoever filled in a 2 at “Don’t talk a lot” gets a 5 after reversing.
The statements are below exactly as they were put to the participants.






ImportantOne row here cannot be — and you only find it by laying two columns side by side



The ages run from 3 to 86. That 3 is odd. But it is not impossible: someone can mistype, or make a joke. Look only at the ages and you see a strange number and nothing more — and you have no grounds at all to do anything with it.
Now look at the column next to it. That same participant ticks the highest level of education: higher education finished, and further study after that. A child of 3 with a university degree. That cannot be.
Mind what just happened. In age there is a strange value; in education a perfectly ordinary one (there are hundreds with the same). Neither column stands out when you look at it on its own. The error is not in a column but between two columns, and by definition you cannot find that by going through the columns one at a time. That is the move you learn here: lay two side by side and ask yourself whether that combination can exist.
How rare that is, in this file: of the 231 participants under eighteen, exactly one gives a level of education you cannot have finished before your eighteenth birthday. That is this one.
And the rest of the young people stay in too. There are 26 twelve-year-olds in this file and 59 sixteen-year-olds. They are real: that is exactly who fills in a personality test on a website. Drawing an age limit because the lowest value is no good would cost 231 people to clear up one row.
And that is why that one row is still in. We have not removed it. Whoever wants it out may take it out — but with the reason alongside, because that is exactly what a researcher is supposed to write down.



What this row is not good for — you can skip this until you get to the assumptions. It looks like a textbook example of a point that pulls the regression line askew, and it is not. Recomputed on neuroticism ~ age: with this participant the slope is −0.011920, without them −0.011893. That is a difference of 0.2 per cent, and you will not see it in any output.
That is not because the row is ordinary. It lies far out, in fact: its age is the lowest of all. On the measure of exactly that — leverage, how far an observation sits from the rest along the x-axis — it scores 0.0024, and that is more than the 0.0023 above which leverage usually counts as striking. So it really is a leverage point, and it is not even the only one: 92 participants pass that line.
But lying far out is not the same as pulling. Its neuroticism score is 3.8 and the line predicts 3.5 for it — it sits almost exactly where the line expects it, and there is nothing to shift about a point that lies on the line. The measure that takes those two things together is Cook’s D: far out on the x-axis and far from the line. Here it is 0.000095, where the rule of thumb only starts to beep at 1.
So the lesson is in two parts, and they are often mixed up. Far out on the x-axis (leverage) and shifting the line (influence) are not the same thing; the first is a condition for the second, not proof of it. And a point weighs, in any case, in proportion to how few other points there are: with 2634 observations that share is tiny, however odd the observation itself. If you want to see what one point can do to a line, you need a small file — that is what the twelve stones are for. This row belongs to checking your data, before you start computing.

title: Exercise 3.3 · Looking at the residuals
text:
Twenty-two penguins of exactly 190 millimetres
prediction · miss
The penguins are old acquaintances — in Exercise 3.2 you drew a line through them yourself: the weight predicted from the flipper length, nearly fifty grams of penguin per millimetre of flipper, and R² = .76.1 Three quarters of all the difference in weight runs along with the flipper. That’s a lot, for living animals, and it sounds as if the line now more or less knows the weight.
And now something odd. The file holds twenty-two penguins with a flipper of exactly 190 millimetres. The line knows only the flipper length, so all twenty-two get the same prediction: 3659.4 grams. What the scales actually said, in grams:

3050 · 3325 · 3400 · 3450 · 3450 · 3450 · 3575 · 3600 · 3600 · 3650 · 3700 · 3700 · 3725 · 3800 · 3900 · 3900 · 3900 · 3950 · 4250 · 4250 · 4250 · 4600

From 3050 to 4600 — a kilo and a half of difference, at one and the same flipper length. The line can do nothing about that: it knows just one thing about a penguin, and that one thing was the same twenty-two times over.
And those twenty-two are no oddity you just happened to hit on. Pick another flipper length and you see the same thing, only with fewer animals in a huddle at once: all along the line, reality sits above it and below it. That sharpens a question we’ve left to one side until now: how far is the line off, penguin by penguin — and what can you do with those misses?
Come along for a moment. The line has had its guess; now we mark its work.

play with it

title: Exercise 3.3 · Looking at the residuals
section: Work out the misses on the twelve stones
text:
Work out the misses on the twelve stones
residual · predicted value
You’ve already seen a miss like that written down in the book: DATA = FIT + RESIDUAL. The fit is what the line guesses, the residual is what’s left over — the miss, now no longer measured from the mean but from the line.
You’ll come across this one thing under four names: miss, residual, deviation, and, in software output and in articles, error. Each time it’s the distance between what is really there and what the line guessed. In this exercise it’s called the miss; when JASP says Residual or a plot says residual, it’s exactly the same thing.






NoteFirst as in the book — the twelve stones · JASP 0.99.0



Open stones.csv and make two columns in the R box (type Scale; after the name Create Column, after the line Compute column), as in the toolbox: left of the arrow the name of the column, right of it what goes in the R box.
guess      ->   fitted(lm(shine ~ carat))
residual   ->   resid(lm(shine ~ carat))
Copy the right-hand side exactly; you don’t have to read it. The top one says “give me what the line guesses”, the bottom one “give me what is left over”. Rounded to one decimal:
guess       30.7   33.9   33.9   40.4   50.0   50.0   53.2   56.4   59.6   59.6   66.1   66.1
residual   -10.7   -3.9   -3.9  -10.4    0.0   20.0   26.8    3.6   10.4   20.4  -36.1  -16.1
Then add up residual: Descriptives, residual in Variables, and under Statistics the Sum tick box.
Check whether that sum comes to zero for you too — give or take a little rounding dust. If it doesn’t, somewhere along the way you’ve got hold of something other than the residuals of this model.


Those are exactly the two columns from the table in the book: Else lands on zero (the line runs straight through her), Kees is furthest off, at −36.1. New is only the picture below — you set those two columns against each other instead of reading them:






NoteIn JASP · the misses in a picture · JASP 0.99.0



Run Regression → Linear Regression with shine as Dependent Variable and carat in Covariates, and under Plots tick the option Residuals vs. predicted: the guess on the horizontal axis, the miss on the vertical one, and the zero line straight through it.


Look closely at what that picture does. The regression line has gone flat: everything the line already knew has been calculated out, so what’s left over should hover around the zero line. A residual plot is a scatterplot swept clean — you’re no longer looking at the association, you’re looking at what the association left behind.






NoteFirst the twelve stones



Two questions before you read on.
a) Ask for the standard deviation of shine, and that of the residuals. (two numbers, and one sentence on what the difference between the two means)
b) Put two columns next to the data: how far each shine lies from the mean (the deviation column from Exercise 1.1, the blue stroke in the book), and the residual (the burgundy stroke). Square both of those columns and add up each column of squares. (two sums, and say what share of the first is swallowed by the second)








CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





a) Shine itself spreads with SD = 21.74 shine points, the residuals with SD = 17.75. Without the line your best guess for every stone is the mean, and how widely the misses fan out around that mean is what the standard deviation of shine sums up: nearly 22 shine points. Guess with the line, and the residuals fan out around the line instead, and that fan is narrower: nearly 18. So the line does save you something, but not much — with these twelve stones, carat is nowhere near everything.
Don’t confuse that 17.75 with the 18.61 from Exercise 3.2, the number the regression itself prints for the spread around the line. Both come from the same squares of the residuals, the ones you add up in b). A standard deviation divides them by eleven, n − 1, because the mean costs one number; the 18.61 divides by ten, n − 2, because the line costs two (the intercept and the slope). Both then take the square root. In the book that second one is called the standard error of the estimate, Se. If someone asks for the standard error of the estimate, it’s that one: 18.61.






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives with shine and residual: Std. Deviation 21.742 and 17.746.
The 18.61 from Exercise 3.2 is in the Model Summary of your regression, under RMSE: 18.613.


b) Shine around its own mean gives 5200.0; shine around the line gives 3464.3. So of all the difference in shine, two thirds is left over once the line has had its share — and the one third it does take is exactly the R² = .33 you saw in Exercises 3.1 and 3.2.






NoteIn JASP



You already have residual. Make three more columns in the R box (type Scale):
deviation    ->   shine - mean(shine)
deviation2   ->   deviation^2
residual2      ->   residual^2
Add up the two columns of squares: Descriptives, deviation2 and residual2 in Variables, and under Statistics the Sum tick box. It says 5200.000 and 3464.286.
The same two are in the ANOVA table of your regression, under Sum of Squares: Total 5200.000 and Residual 3464.286. The top row, Regression 1735.714, is the part the line does take.


Why that is so, you’ll find below.

title: Exercise 3.3 · Looking at the residuals
section: The residual, and where R² comes from
text:
The residual, and where R² comes from
residual · residual plot · R²
Look at that sum of the residuals once more. Zero — not roughly, but exactly, give or take rounding. That’s no coincidence and no compliment to the line either: it’s the construction. That’s how the line was laid — for every miss on the plus side there’s just as much on the minus side, because if anything were left over, the whole line could shift a bit, and then it wouldn’t have been the best-fitting line.
Build in small moments to check — it ought to be zero; is it? So do hold on to that zero as a checkpoint: if your column of residuals doesn’t add up to zero, something has gone wrong along the way.
But mind what it also means. Precisely because that sum is always zero — with a line that runs tight through the cloud and with a line that leaves all sorts behind — it says nothing about how well the line guesses. Plus and minus cancel out regardless. If you want to know how well, you mustn’t add up but look: how widely do the misses lie around zero?
And that’s exactly what you see in the residual plot. The twenty-two this exercise opened with stand there as a single column: same guess, twenty-two misses, above and below zero.






NoteIn JASP · draw the misses and count the garden · JASP 0.99.0



Open penguins.csv and run Regression → Linear Regression with body_mass_g as Dependent Variable and flipper_length_mm in Covariates; under Plots, tick Residuals vs. predicted. Then make the same column as with the stones:
residual   ->   resid(lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm))
Descriptives gives you the two numbers you need: body_mass_g spreads with Std. Deviation 801.955, residual with 393.700. Divide one by the other and square, in three small steps you can all check by hand:
393.700 / 801.955 = 0.491
0.491 x 0.491     = 0.241
1 - 0.241         = .759
Mind one number in Model Summary: there it says RMSE 394.278 and not 393.700. Neither is wrong — the RMSE divides by 340 (342 animals minus the two numbers that describe the line, the intercept and the slope), a standard deviation by 341.


Without the line your best guess for every weight was the mean — you know that game. The standard deviation of the weight measures how widely the weights lie around that one guess: 801.95 grams. With the line they lie closer together. The standard deviation of the misses measures how widely they lie around the line: 393.70 grams. So the line makes the spread 408.25 grams narrower, just over half of the spread without the line.
And yet Exercise 3.2 said R² = .76. Three quarters. Who’s lying — the half or the three quarters? Neither; they count in a different measure. Think of all the difference in weight as a garden full of variation. Explaining an association isn’t explaining a length but an area, and area goes in squares — so square the two standard deviations before you divide one by the other. Then it says .24: the part of the garden the line leaves behind, divided by the whole garden. The rest the line does take: one minus .24 is .76. In metres along the edge the line wins just over half; in garden area, three quarters. It’s the same gain, measured twice.
And R² needs nothing new for that: everything it knows is already in the misses. Do the same on the twelve stones and out comes .33 — exactly the square of the r you put together yourself at the start of this chapter, with all its decimals (the rounded .58 squared gives .34). Two routes, one number: square the correlation, or keep the books on the misses.

title: Exercise 3.3 · Looking at the residuals
section: The bookkeeping of the penguin line
text:
The bookkeeping of the penguin line
sum of the residuals · residual plot · R² from the misses
Now you, on the line from the hook: the weight of 342 penguins, predicted from their flipper length. You drew it and read it in Exercise 3.2; now you’re going to work out what it left behind.






NoteIn JASP · set it up · JASP 0.99.0



penguins.csv is open and the regression of body_mass_g on flipper_length_mm is running. One more column to add, next to residual:
guess      ->   fitted(lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm))








NoteYour turn



Answer the questions in order; they build on each other. The last one is deliberately called Z) and not k): the cloud question always comes last.
There are eleven of them, and that’s too many for one sitting. After e) you have the misses in hand and you’ve found the hook again — a good moment to stop. At f) the bookkeeping starts, and that’s the part R² rolls out of.
In brackets, each time, is what belongs in a complete answer. Where it says that a part is up to you, the wording is free — for the rest, the answer is fixed. And under Exam-style questions, at the end of this exercise, the same topics come round once more, in the form an exam would ask them in.
a) Ask for the prediction and the residual of the first six penguins (the first six rows of guess and residual). For one of the six, add the two together and set the result beside its real weight. (two rows of six, and one sum)
b) Add up all 342 residuals. What comes out, and why is that not a compliment to the line? (one number, and two sentences)
c) Draw the residual plot. What should be there, and what do you see? (two sentences)
d) Find the penguin where the line is furthest off, upwards and downwards. (two numbers with their unit, and say which species they are)
e) Back to the twenty-two from the hook. Ask for the residuals of the penguins with a flipper of exactly 190 millimetres. (the smallest and the largest, and one sentence on what stands above that one guess in the residual plot)
f) Now the bookkeeping. Add up the squared deviations of the weight around its own mean, and those of the residuals around zero. Then add up the squared distances from the line to the mean (all three are in the ANOVA table, under Sum of Squares: at Total, Residual and Regression). (three numbers — and add the last two together)
g) Work out R² from those numbers: one minus the residual sum divided by the total sum. Set it beside the R² in Model Summary. (two numbers)
h) Ask for the standard deviation of the weight and that of the residuals. By what percentage does the line make the spread narrower — and why is that a different number from the R² in g)? (two numbers, and two sentences)
i) Colour the residual plot by species and ask for the mean residual per species. What does that say about the line? (three numbers, and two sentences)
j) Write down your finding in one sentence. (what the line covers, and what it leaves behind per penguin — those two have to be in it, the words around them are up to you; more than one answer is right)
Z) Is the cloud straight, and are there no points in it screwing the whole thing up? Look at your residual plot from c) — is there an arc in it, or does one animal hang so far out that it pulls on the line all by itself? (two short statements, and say which of your answers above depend on them)








CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





a) The six predictions are 3212.3 · 3460.7 · 3907.9 · 3808.5 · 3659.4 · 3212.3 grams, and the six residuals 537.7 · 339.3 · −657.9 · −358.5 · −9.4 · 412.7. Add them up per animal and you have the weight back: the first penguin weighs 3212.3 + 537.7 = 3750 grams, and that’s what’s in the file too. DATA = FIT + RESIDUAL, literally.






NoteIn JASP



Look in your data at the first six rows of guess, residual and body_mass_g. If you want them as a table: under Statistics, at Residuals, tick the option Casewise diagnostics and set it to All.


b) Zero, give or take rounding. And that’s no compliment: it’s the way the line was laid. Every miss on the plus side has a miss on the minus side standing opposite it, and that goes for every best-fitting line — including one that’s completely off. A number that’s always the same can’t tell you anything about how well it’s going.






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives with residual, Sum ticked: it says zero, give or take a little rounding dust.


c) What should be there is a shapeless cloud around the zero line: everything the line already knew has been calculated out, so what’s left over may no longer carry any pattern. And at first sight that’s what you see, too — a band of points that stays about equally wide from left to right and nowhere clearly runs up or down; at Z) you look more closely. What you do see is the vertical stripes: penguins were measured to whole millimetres, so the guesses land on a limited number of spots.
d) Upwards the line is off by 1288.69 grams (an Adelie, row 39) and downwards by 1058.80 grams (a Chinstrap, row 313). A good kilo, both of them — on animals that weigh a good four kilos on average.






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives with residual gives Minimum −1058.797 and Maximum 1288.687. Which two animals those are, you find with the filter: residual == max(residual) leaves one row, and there you read off the species. Switch the filter off again afterwards.


e) From −609 to +941 grams. So in the residual plot, above that one guess of 3659.4, stands a single vertical stripe of twenty-two points, a good kilo and a half tall. That’s the hook, now as a picture: the same prediction, twenty-two different misses.






NoteIn JASP



Put flipper_length_mm == 190 in the filter — 22 animals remain — and ask for the Minimum and Maximum of residual: −609.426 and 940.574. Switch the filter off again afterwards.


f) The total sum is 219 307 697, the residual sum 52 854 796 and the fit sum 166 452 902. Add those last two together and you get the first one back. That’s DATA = FIT + RESIDUAL, but in squared deviations — and that is the form in which the bookkeeping balances.
Check it by hand and you come out one too high: 166 452 902 + 52 854 796 is 219 307 698, and above it says 219 307 697. That’s no crack in the bookkeeping but rounding crumbs — all three sums were rounded separately, and unrounded they coincide, give or take machine noise.






NoteIn JASP



All three are in the ANOVA table, under Sum of Squares: Total 219307697.368, Residual 52854795.628 and Regression 166452901.740. Those are the same three numbers as above, only without the spaces and with three decimals after them.


g) .76, both of them.






NoteIn JASP



Working it out yourself: 1 − 52854795.628 / 219307697.368 = .759 — your own number, so without the zero in front. And in Model Summary it says 0.759, because JASP does carry its zero along.


And that’s the point of this exercise. R² is not a separate measure that JASP conjures up from somewhere: it’s the garden the line takes, divided by the whole garden. You’ve just worked it out from the misses yourself.
h) The standard deviation of the weight is 801.95 grams, that of the residuals 393.70. So the line makes the spread 408.25 grams narrower, and that’s 51 per cent of the spread without the line — just over half, not three quarters.
Two sentences on why both those numbers are right: the 51 per cent counts in grams, along the edge of the garden, and the .76 counts in area. Squaring turns just over half into three quarters — check it: 393.70 divided by 801.95 is .49, and .49 squared is .24, and one minus .24 is .76.






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives with body_mass_g and residual: Std. Deviation 801.955 and 393.700. (The RMSE of 394.278 in Model Summary is a different number — see the box above, at the garden.)


i) Adelie +43.5, Chinstrap −215.7, Gentoo +65.8 grams.






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives, residual in Variables and species in Split: 43.539, −215.683 and 65.789 grams. The coloured residual plot you make in that same Descriptives: take residual out of Variables for a moment, then put in first guess and then residual (the first one goes on the horizontal axis), leave species in Split and, under Customizable Plots, tick Scatter plots.


Two sentences: across all 342 the mean residual is zero, but per species it isn’t — for the Chinstraps the line sits systematically a good two hundred grams too high, and for the other two a little too low. That means there’s a third player in the cloud here too, exactly as in Exercise 3.1; only this time it’s small enough not to tip the line over.
j) For example:

The line of weight on flipper length covered just over three quarters of the differences in weight among 342 penguins (R² = .76), but still left nearly four hundred grams of spread behind per animal (SD of the residuals = 393.70).

Z) Half and half — and the half that doesn’t hold, you know already.
There’s a slight arc in it. A slanting stripe can’t be in it: the association between the guess and the miss is exactly zero, and that’s no finding but the construction — that’s precisely what “the line has gone flat” means. An arc can. Look carefully at your plot from c): at the low and the high guesses the points lie on average a little above the zero line, in the middle on average below it. That’s the dip from Exercise 3.2 — +57, −106 and +41 grams per third of flipper length — now as a picture instead of as three numbers. You can barely see it, and that’s why 3.2 worked it out for you. Where it comes from, you know already too: from the species. At i) the line sat a good two hundred grams too high for the Chinstraps, on average.
And no penguin pulls on the line all by itself. The biggest miss is 1288.69 grams, and that’s a good three times the standard deviation of the residuals — an animal that stands out, but not one that tips the line. Leave it out and the slope barely moves.






NoteIn JASP



Regression → Correlation with guess and residual: Pearson’s r 0.000 — exactly zero, give or take machine noise.


What hangs on it: little here, because the arc is slight. Had it been stronger, the whole bookkeeping would still stand — the sums at f), the R² at g), the standard deviations at h) and the species means at i) are sums over these 342 animals, and those stay right whatever is bent. What you would then redo is every sentence in which you recommend the line: at j) it says it covers three quarters, and if the association runs strongly curved, that’s no lie, but it is a line that lets you down in the wrong place.

The same bookkeeping on 2634 questionnaires
scale score · R² from the misses · the sample sentence






NoteFinal task



The last word of the whole chapter, and it ends where this book always ends: with people.
bigfive.csv holds 2634 people who rated twenty-five statements about themselves on a scale from 1 to 6. You use ten of them here — five on neuroticism, how easily you get upset, and five on openness, the taste for new things. You met them in Exercises 3.1 and 3.2, with O2 and O5 reversed first; now you do this exercise’s bookkeeping on them.

Open bigfive.csv and make three columns in the R box (type Scale), as in the toolbox: left of the arrow the name of the column, right of it what goes in the R box.
neuroticism   ->   rowMeans(data.frame(N1, N2, N3, N4, N5))

Then run Regression → Linear Regression with neuroticism as Dependent Variable and openness in Covariates.


a) Ask for the residuals and add them up. (one number, and one sentence on why you could have predicted that)
b) Ask for the standard deviation of neuroticism and that of the residuals. How much does the line save you? (two numbers, and one sentence)
c) Work out R² from the misses, just as with the penguins. (one number, and set it beside the R² in Model Summary)
d) Now the people version of the twenty-two penguins. How many people score exactly 4.0 on openness, what prediction do they all get, and how far apart does their real neuroticism run? (three answers, and one sentence)
e) Write down what you’ve found, in two sentences and in this fixed form:

Within these n people: … (R² = …). Whether that also holds beyond these n, you don’t know yet.

(fill in the n, the finding in plain words and the R² — and leave that second sentence exactly as it stands; for the finding, more than one answer is right)








CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





a) Zero, give or take rounding — and you could have predicted that, because it holds for every best-fitting line, however well or badly it fits. It was so with the diamonds, it was so with the penguins, and so it is here.






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives with residual_people, Sum ticked: zero, give or take a little rounding dust.


b) Neuroticism spreads with SD = 1.1946 scale points, the residuals with SD = 1.1897. So the line saves you 0.0049 of a scale point on a scale from 1 to 6 — in other words: next to nothing. (Four decimals here on purpose: at two you can’t even see the difference any more.) Whoever knows someone’s openness knows hardly any more about their neuroticism than whoever knows only the mean.






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives: Std. Deviation 1.195 for neuroticism and 1.190 for residual_people. If you want to see the four decimals from the text — 1.1946 and 1.1897 — set Preferences → Results → Fix the number of decimals to 4.


c) .01, both of them. Of the whole garden this line takes barely one per cent.






NoteIn JASP



1 − 1.1897² / 1.1946² = .008 — your own number, without the zero in front. In Model Summary it says 0.008.


d) 188 people score exactly 4.0 on openness. All 188 of them get the same prediction: 3.24 scale points of neuroticism. And their real neuroticism runs from 1.0 to 6.0 — from the lowest score that exists on this scale to the highest, all within that one guess.






NoteIn JASP



Put openness == 4 in the filter: 188 rows remain, and that count is in Descriptives at Valid. For neuroticism it says Minimum 1.000 and Maximum 6.000 there. The prediction you work out yourself from the two numbers in Coefficients: 3.774 − 0.133 × 4 = 3.242. Switch the filter off again afterwards.


That’s the same figure as the twenty-two penguins this exercise opened with, only harder: there the real weight ran across a kilo and a half at one guess, here the real neuroticism runs across the whole scale at one guess. With people that’s the rule, not the exception.
e) For example:

Within these 2634 people: whoever is more open scores on average slightly lower on neuroticism, but openness and neuroticism share barely one per cent of their differences (R² = .01). Whether that also holds beyond these 2634, you don’t know yet.

Look at what that second sentence does. Everything you’ve worked out in this chapter — the covariance, the correlation, the line, the residuals, the R² — describes the people in front of you, and nobody else. You’ve been given no reason at all to assume that the next 2634 people would show the same, and no way either of saying how likely that is.
That is exactly where the next movement begins.

title: Exercise 3.3 · Looking at the residuals
text:
Exam-style questions
DATA = FIT + RESIDUAL · R² from the misses · residual plot
These six have the form an exam would ask this topic in: four options, and exactly one is the best — the other three may well be true and still not be the best answer. Only questions 2 and 3 need any arithmetic.






NoteExam-style questions



1. You add up all 342 misses of the line and zero comes out. What may you conclude from that about how well this line guesses?

Nothing: with every best-fitting line that sum is zero, even with a line that’s completely off.
The line fits well: the misses above and below the line keep each other neatly in balance.
The R² must be 1, because on balance nothing is left over.
The line guesses neither too high nor too low on average, and that’s exactly what you want from a good line.

2. One of the twenty-two penguins with a flipper of 190 millimetres weighs 4250 grams. The line predicts 3659.4 grams for all twenty-two. How big is the miss for this animal?

−590.6 grams
590.6 grams
4250.0 grams
7909.4 grams

3. For the line of weight on flipper length, the total sum of the squared deviations is 219 307 697 and the residual sum 52 854 796. What is the R² of this line?

.24
.51
.76
3.15

4. The standard deviation of the weight is 801.95 grams, that of the misses 393.70 grams. In grams, then, the line makes the spread 51 per cent narrower, while the R² is .76. Which statement about those two numbers is the best?

One of the two must be wrong; the same gain can’t have two numbers.
The 51 per cent counts in grams and the .76 in squared grams; it’s the same gain, measured twice.
The .76 belongs to the line and the 51 per cent to the misses, so they’re about different things.
The .76 is too optimistic: 51 per cent is what the line really saves you, and the R² inflates that by squaring.

5. You draw the residual plot: the guess on one axis, the miss on the other. What should be there, and what does it mean if there is a pattern in it?

A rising cloud — the miss should run along with the guess; if it lies flat, something has gone wrong.
A shapeless cloud around the zero line; a pattern means the line has left something behind that it could have taken along.
A shapeless cloud around the zero line; a pattern means there are measurement errors in the file.
A falling cloud — big guesses always go with smaller misses.

6. You ask for the mean miss per species and it says: Adelie +43.5, Chinstrap −215.7 and Gentoo +65.8 grams. Yet the mean miss over all 342 animals is zero. Which statement is the best?

Those can’t both be true: three means that aren’t zero can’t add up to zero between them.
The line is useless for Chinstraps and must be drawn separately for that species.
The species carries information the line doesn’t have: within a group the balance may tilt, even though over all 342 animals it stands at zero.
The three species differ too much in size, and so the biggest species pulls the mean towards zero.









CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





1 a · 2 b · 3 c · 4 b · 5 b · 6 c
Below, for each question, is why — and why the other three options are tempting. If you got one right, you can skip it.
1. a. That zero is the construction and not the outcome: that’s how the line was laid. A number that’s always the same can’t tell you anything about what differs. b reads the balance as a compliment, and that’s the trap — plus and minus cancel out with a line that leaves all sorts behind, too. c confuses nothing on balance with nothing: the misses aren’t zero, their sum is zero, and the R² is .76. d is the trickiest, because the statement is true — the line guesses neither too high nor too low on average — and precisely because of that it says nothing: it holds for every best-fitting line, so it distinguishes this line from nothing.
2. b. DATA = FIT + RESIDUAL, so the miss is what’s really there minus what the line guessed: 4250 − 3659.4 = 590.6 grams. a has the sign the wrong way round and computes fit minus data; then this animal would be lighter than predicted, while it’s heavier. c names the weight itself. d adds instead of subtracting: 4250 + 3659.4 = 7909.4, and that’s heavier than the heaviest penguin in the file.
3. c. One minus the residual sum divided by the total sum: 1 − 52 854 796 / 219 307 697 = .76. a is the division without that one-minus in front — .24 is exactly the part the line does not take, and that’s exactly why the minus is there. b is the 51 per cent from question 4, the number in grams rather than in squared grams. d divides the fit sum by the residual sum: 166 452 902 / 52 854 796 = 3.15. A share coming out above 1 is your clue that something hasn’t been divided by the total.
4. b. Think of all the difference in weight as a garden: along the edge the line wins just over half, in area three quarters. Area goes in squares, so square first and then divide. a looks for a mistake where there is none; both numbers can be checked. c sets the line and the misses against each other, but they come from the same bookkeeping — the R² was worked out from the misses. d calls squaring an inflating move. It’s a choice of measure, and it’s the measure that explaining an association comes in: area, not length.
5. b. Everything the line already knew has been calculated out, so what’s left over may no longer carry any pattern — and if there is a pattern in it, then there was still something in the misses the line could have used. a and d expect a direction in the residual plot, and there can’t be one: with a best-fitting line the association between the guess and the miss is exactly zero. That the plot is flat is therefore no sign that something has gone wrong, but the intention. c has the right cloud and the wrong conclusion: a pattern points to something the model is missing, not to faults in the scales.
Note that pattern has two guises here, and you meet both. A pattern along the axis is an arc, or a fan that gets wider: then the miss goes with the height of the guess. A pattern per group is what you work out at i): within one species the misses lie on one side on average, while over all 342 animals together they come out at zero. The second you don’t see if you don’t colour the points — and that’s exactly why i) asks you to.
6. c. Over all 342 animals the mean miss is zero, because that’s how the line was laid — but within a group that balance is quite free to tilt. That the Chinstraps are systematically a good two hundred grams off means the species knows something the line doesn’t: the third player from 3.1, now visible in the misses. a is too quick: negative and positive do add up to zero between them, and these are unequal groups besides (151, 68 and 123 animals), so it doesn’t even count with the same number of animals per species. b jumps from an observation to an intervention; two hundred grams on an animal of a good three and a half kilos is small, and this exercise deliberately lets that line stand. d has the biggest species pulling the mean towards zero, and that’s the wrong way round: the zero isn’t there in spite of the species but by construction.
The numbers in these six questions all appear earlier on this page. What’s new is the miss in question 2 and the wrong distractors — and those are all written out above as sums, so you can check them without having to take them on trust.

text:
Longer bill, shallower bill?
association · negative r
Somewhere on a bare rock off Antarctica stands someone with a pair of callipers and 342 penguins who never asked for any of it.1 Of every penguin he writes down two things: how long the bill is, and how deep. By deep we mean the height of the bill — top to bottom, seen from the side, not the width and not the length. Nothing more: two numbers per animal, neatly one under the other.



The bill in profile: length runs from front to back, depth is the height from top to bottom.


And now us. Because something odd is hiding in those two columns. Work out the association between bill length and bill depth across all 342 penguins and out comes a number that is negative: r = −.24. In plain words: the longer the bill, the less deep — as if an animal with a long nose must have a thin nose.
Does that feel right? Not to me. Come along for a moment — we’re going to find out for ourselves, and on the way that number turns out to say something quite different from what it seems.

title: Exercise 3.1 · Correlation and the scatterplot
section: Where r comes from — the twelve stones first
text:
Where r comes from — the twelve stones first
covariance · sum of products
Two columns, twelve stones: carat and shine, neatly side by side. And you want one number that says how those two move together. Half the work you’ve already done in the book — for every stone you know its deviation from the mean, the blue strokes. Only here every stone has two: one on carat (the mean is 1.60) and one on shine (mean 50.00).
Then the move you know from the book: multiply those two deviations by each other, stone by stone. If they point the same way — both above, or both below — plus comes out; if they contradict each other, minus.
Do two by hand and you’ll see it happen. The twelve stones have names in the book, and two of them serve well here. Anna weighs 1.0 carat and shines 20, so her deviations are −0.6 carats and −30 shine points: both below the mean, and minus times minus is plus. Her contribution is +18. Kees weighs 2.1 carats and shines 30 — heavy, but dull. His deviations are +0.5 and −20; those contradict each other, and his contribution is −10.




carat deviation

The other ten you don’t have to do by hand. In the first box below you rebuild the rectangle part of the table from the book’s rectangle section, as three columns beside the data: the deviation on carat, the deviation on shine, and the two multiplied together. Then look in your own third column: eight stones push the sum up, three sit exactly on a mean and so count zero, and only Kees counts against. Add that column up and you get 54 — that sum is called the sum of products. Divide by n − 1 = 11, and there it is: the covariance (Sxy), 4.91. The average rectangle.
And now the question you should ask of every number: 4.91 what? Just carry the unit along — a deviation in carats times a deviation in shine is… carat-shines. Is 4.91 carat-shines a lot of association? You can’t say. Nobody thinks in carat-shines. Raw is rubbish. The covariance still sits on the scale of its two variables; you can read the direction off it — plus, so heavier goes with shinier — but not the strength.
The repair is one division. Divide the covariance by the two standard deviations — 0.3908 carats and 21.7423 shine points — and watch what happens to the units: carat cancels against carat, shine against shine. What’s left is a bare number without a unit, the standardised version of the same association, and that number can never get outside −1 and +1: r = .58. That you can read in one go, with diamonds just as well as with penguins.






NoteFirst as in the book — build the correlation yourself · JASP 0.99.0



Open stones.csv and rebuild the table from the book, as three columns: click the + to the right of the last column, give it a name, choose type Scale and the R icon, and click Create Column; then you type the rule and click Compute column. That is how the toolbox has it too. In the boxes below, left of the arrow is the name of the column and right of it what you type in the R box; you don’t type the arrow itself.
dev_carat   ->   carat - mean(carat)
dev_shine    ->   shine - mean(shine)
rectangle    ->   dev_carat * dev_shine
Add the rectangles up: Descriptives, rectangle in Variables, and under Statistics the Sum tick box. It says 54.000. Divide by eleven on your calculator: 54 / 11 = 4.909, the 4.91 from the text above.
Then the same in one go, and standardised straight away — two more columns:
S_xy     ->   cov(carat, shine)
r_self   ->   cov(carat, shine) / (sd(carat) * sd(shine))
Copy the right-hand side exactly; you don’t have to read it. The top one says “give me the covariance”, the bottom one “and divide that by the two standard deviations”.
In S_xy every row holds the same number: 4.909, your average rectangle, with the third decimal that JASP shows by default. In r_self it says 0.578; there the unit has been divided out.
Then the same with one click: Regression → Correlation, carat and shine in Variables, Pearson’s r ticked (it already is), and under Plots the Scatter plots. Next to Pearson’s r it says 0.578.
And which line goes with it: Regression → Linear Regression, shine as Dependent Variable and carat in Covariates. In Coefficients it says (Intercept) −1.429 and carat 32.143.


So Correlation is no black box: it’s your covariance, divided by your two standard deviations. JASP just does the cancelling faster.
Mind the difference between what your screen says and what you write down yourself. JASP prints 0.578, zero and all; in the text above it says r = .58. That’s not sloppiness on either side. A click path quotes your screen; your own sentence follows APA, and there you leave the zero off because its absence says something: this number can’t get past 1. The numbers in the JASP boxes of this exercise book are therefore as JASP shows them, so you can check whether you have the same thing in front of you. Square that r with all the decimals on your screen and you have r² = .33 — a third of the differences in shine runs along with the weight, the rest doesn’t. (Square the rounded .58 and you get .34: here too, whoever calculates on with a printed number calculates the rounding along with it.)






NoteFirst the twelve stones



Two questions before you read on, and then you can be let loose on something new.
a) A carat is just a weight: 200 milligrams. So weigh the stones in milligrams (make a column mg with carat * 200) and ask for the covariance again. (one number, and one sentence on what has and hasn’t changed about the twelve stones)
b) Divide that new covariance by the two standard deviations that now go with it. (one number, and say what you recognise)








CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





a) 981.82 milligram-shines — two hundred times the covariance of a moment ago. (Work out 200 × 4.91 by hand and you get 982.00; JASP multiplies the unrounded 4.9091. The same kind of gap as anywhere you calculate on with a printed number.) And nothing about the stones has changed: not one weight, not one shine, not one point in the cloud. Only the unit you write the weight in is different. A number that becomes two hundred times as big the moment you pick a different unit can’t say how strong an association is.






NoteIn JASP · the stones in milligrams



mg        ->   carat * 200
S_xy_mg   ->   cov(mg, shine)
Out comes 981.818.


b) .58 — the same number as a moment ago. Dividing by the standard deviations takes the unit out, and that’s exactly why the correlation exists.






NoteIn JASP · and standardised again



r_mg      ->   cov(mg, shine) / (sd(mg) * sd(shine))
It says 0.578, exactly what r_self gave too.





Now you — on the penguins, which you know by now. A new question for familiar animals: does the length of a bill go with its depth?
Bring the penguins in and throw them into a picture. One dot per penguin: bill length on one axis, bill depth on the other.






NoteIn JASP · give it a tug · JASP 0.99.0




Open penguins.csv (menu top left → Open).
Regression → Correlation, and drag bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm to Variables. Leave Pearson’s r ticked.
In the small menu under Regression, Correlation appears twice. You want the top one, under Classical.
Under Plots, tick Scatter plots: 342 dots, a cloud.

Next to Pearson’s r it says −0.235.


There it is: a cloud that hangs from top left to bottom right, and the number −0.235 is one figure for “how tightly does that cloud tilt down?”. The scale runs from −1 (a perfect falling line) through 0 (no straight-line association) to +1 (a perfect rising line). −.24 is a gentle fall with a lot of clutter around it — weak, but it’s there. Longer bill, shallower bill. Says the number.

title: Exercise 3.1 · Correlation and the scatterplot
text:
Three species in one cloud
confounding · third player · flipped sign · r²
The temptation now is to write: “in penguins, a longer bill goes with a shallower one.” The number has been worked out properly, the sentence seems to follow. And yet it’s wrong. Colour the cloud by species:






NoteIn JASP · colour the cloud · JASP 0.99.0




Colouring by group is something Correlation can’t do; Descriptives → Descriptive Statistics does it. Put bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm under Variables there (the first one goes on the horizontal axis) and species under Split, and under Customizable Plots tick Scatter plots. JASP then colours the dots by species, and draws a line of its own for each species. Leave the Correlation from before open: the new table and cloud come in below it, and you need it again in the next step.
JASP cuts off the legend next to the cloud by itself, even if you make the picture bigger in JASP: you only see Ad, Ch and Ge, with the first letters of species above them. Those are Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo.
And now work out r separately within one species: click the funnel above the data, and then, bottom left in the filter window, on R (if the R box is already there, skip that). Put species == "Gentoo" in place of the bottom line, and click Apply pass-through filter. Below the data it then says Data has 342 rows, 123 (~36%) passed through filter. The Correlation recalculates, and next to Pearson’s r it says 0.643.
That number is in the Correlation from before, higher up on your results page.
Then switch the filter off again — otherwise everything after this is worked out on the Gentoos.



Suddenly you see it. There are three species in that cloud, each as a huddle of its own. And within each huddle the association runs the other way: longer bill, deeper bill. Check it — Adelie +.39, Chinstrap +.65, Gentoo +.64. All three positive. The sign has flipped.
What happened? The Adelies (top left) have short, deep bills, the Gentoos (bottom right) long, shallow ones; the Chinstraps sit top right, with long and deep ones, though there are only 68 of them. Throw them all on one heap and the difference between the Adelies and the Gentoos drags the whole cloud down at a slant — and that’s where the −.24 comes from. Not from an association between bill length and bill depth, but from the difference between the species. The species is a third player dressing itself up as the association. The book calls that confounding later on; you saw it happen here, in the colours of a scatterplot.
And that’s the double lesson of this exercise, finer than either on its own:

The calculator said: across these 342 animals, r is exactly −.24. There’s nothing to argue with there; check it yourself.
The scatterplot said: true — but not what you think. The direction is a mirage of the species.

So worked out and true are two different things. A correlation can be right to the last decimal and still point you the wrong way. That’s why you never read r without the cloud beside it — and certainly not without asking who else is in that cloud. If you had to write it down in one honest sentence, then not “longer bills are shallower”, but: across three species the cloud hangs downwards, but within each species upwards — the minus sign is a species effect.
(And that small number r² you sometimes see — here .06 — is the “share of shared variance”: of all the difference in bill depth, only a few per cent shares anything with bill length. That too is no “explanation”, only bookkeeping.)

title: Exercise 3.1 · Correlation and the scatterplot
text:
From bill to flipper
computing a correlation · colouring by species · species difference
From bill to flipper. penguins.csv also holds the columns flipper_length_mm (in mm) and body_mass_g (in grams). Same recipe, different question: do those two go together?






NoteIn JASP · set it up · JASP 0.99.0



Open penguins.csv. The covariances you make in the R box, as with the stones; the correlation and the cloud come from Regression → Correlation, and the means per species from Descriptives.








NoteYour turn



Answer the questions in order; they build on each other. The first three are the route you saw run on the twelve stones above — raw, and only then standardised. The last one is deliberately called Z) and not k): the cloud question always comes last.
There are eleven of them, and that’s too many for one sitting. After f) you’ll have made a whole correlation from start to finish — a good moment to stop and dive back in tomorrow. At g) something else begins: there it’s no longer about the number but about who is in the cloud.
In brackets, each time, is what belongs in a complete answer. Where it says more than one answer is right, or that a part is up to you, the wording is free — for the rest, the answer is fixed. And under Exam-style questions, at the end of this exercise, the same topics come round once more, in the form an exam would ask them in.
a) Work out the covariance between flipper length and weight. (report Sxy with its unit — and that unit is two words long)
b) Do the same again, but put the weight in kilos first (make a column kg with body_mass_g / 1000). (the new number, and one sentence on why this is a problem for a measure that is supposed to express strength)
c) Divide both your covariances by the two standard deviations that go with them. (two numbers, and say what has happened to the unit)
d) Draw the cloud. (one sentence on which way it leans and how tightly — the direction is fixed, how tightly is your call)
e) Say in plain words what the sign means here. (one sentence, about penguins — the direction is fixed, the wording is up to you; a number may go in if you say what it measures)
f) Square the correlation. (report r², and one sentence on what that number does say and what it doesn’t)
g) Don’t trust that number before you’ve seen the species. Colour the cloud by species and work out r separately within each species. (three correlations, each with its n)
h) And yet the r across all 342 is higher than within any species on its own. How can that be?
Do it in two steps. First ask for the mean weight and the mean flipper length per species — six numbers, one Descriptives with species in Split. Then look at those six and try to say what makes the Gentoos different. (two or three sentences; if you can’t work it out, the answer below isn’t a defeat; it’s the point)
i) With the bills above, the sign flipped; here it didn’t. What’s the difference? (two sentences)
j) Write down your finding in one honest sentence. (N, both variables, the r across everything and the range within the species — those four have to be in it, the words around them are up to you; more than one answer is right)
Z) Is the cloud straight, and are there no points in it screwing the whole thing up? An r sums up one thing: how tightly the points lie around a straight line. So look back at your cloud from d) — does it bend anywhere, and is there one point hanging so far out that it’s pulling on the number all by itself? (two short statements, and say which of your answers above depend on them)








CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





a) Sxy = 9824.42 millimetre-grams. Four digits before the point, and a unit you’ll meet nowhere else.






NoteIn JASP



S_fm      ->   cov(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)
Out comes 9824.416.


b) In kilos it’s 9.8244 millimetre-kilograms. Exactly a thousand times smaller, because you’ve put numbers a thousand times smaller in one of the columns — and nothing else. Not one penguin has changed weight, not one point has shifted in the cloud, and yet a different number now stands there. A measure that depends on your scales can’t say how strong an association is.






NoteIn JASP



kg        ->   body_mass_g / 1000
S_fkg     ->   cov(flipper_length_mm, kg)
Out comes 9.824 — to the four decimals of the answer above, that is 9.8244.


c) Both .87. The standard deviation of flipper length is 14.0617 mm, that of weight 801.9545 g, and that of weight in kilos 0.8020 kg. Divide the covariance by the product of the two that go with it and you get the same bare number twice.
And that’s because the unit is gone. On top of the fraction were millimetre-grams; underneath is millimetre times gram. They cancel each other out, and what’s left can no longer know what unit you weighed in.






NoteIn JASP



r_fm      ->   cov(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) / (sd(flipper_length_mm) * sd(body_mass_g))
r_fkg     ->   cov(flipper_length_mm, kg) / (sd(flipper_length_mm) * sd(kg))
Both 0.871. The same 0.871 appears in Regression → Correlation under Pearson’s r.


d) A tight rising cloud, from bottom left to top right, and far less clutter around it than with the bills.






NoteIn JASP



The cloud: Regression → Correlation with flipper_length_mm and body_mass_g, and under Plots the Scatter plots on.


e) Penguins with longer flippers are heavier. Nothing more — it doesn’t say the flipper makes the weight.
f) r² = .76. Three quarters of all the difference in weight runs along with flipper length. What it is not: an explanation. It’s bookkeeping — which part of the differences the two measures share, not why they do.
g) Adelie r = .47 (n = 151), Chinstrap r = .64 (n = 68), Gentoo r = .70 (n = 123).






NoteIn JASP



Colour the cloud in Descriptives → Descriptive Statistics: flipper_length_mm and body_mass_g under Variables, species under Split, and under Customizable Plots tick Scatter plots. Then, with the funnel, switch on one species at a time: species == "Adelie", and so on. Next to Pearson’s r it says 0.468, 0.642 and 0.703. Then switch the filter off again.


h) Keep your coloured picture from g) at hand — the answer is in there, and the six numbers below only say what you see on it. Ask for them:






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives, with body_mass_g and flipper_length_mm in Variables and species in Split. It says 3700.662 · 3733.088 · 5076.016 grams and 189.954 · 195.824 · 217.187 mm.


Now look at what the Gentoos are: by far the heaviest animals (5076 grams against 3701 and 3733) and the longest flippers (217.2 mm against 190.0 and 195.8). Heavy and long-flippered — that is the same direction as the association within each species. So the species difference pushes the cloud along that diagonal instead of standing across it.
And then, across all 342, you’re adding two things together: the association within each species, and the jump from one species to the next. Two huddles that already lie at a slant and moreover lie apart from each other along that same diagonal make, together, one long tight cloud — tighter than either huddle on its own.
If you want to see how big that jump is, set it beside the clutter within a species — but that’s an extra storey on top of your answer, not something you should have got out of the six numbers:






NoteIn JASP



jump    ->   sd(tapply(body_mass_g, species, mean))
clutter    ->   sqrt(mean(tapply(body_mass_g, species, var)))
Out come 784.868 and 451.711 — the 785 and 452 that the answer below goes on to calculate with, rounded to whole grams.


So the jump between the species is a good one and a half times the clutter within one species (785 divided by 452 is 1.74), and that whole stretch counts fully in that .87.
i) With the bills, the species difference lay across the association within the species: the Gentoos have long and shallow bills, while within each species a longer bill is a deeper one. There the species pushed the cloud the other way, and the sign flipped. Here the species difference lies along it, and then it strengthens what is already happening within the species. Same third player, two opposite outcomes — and that’s exactly why the sign alone isn’t enough.
j) For example:

In 342 penguins, flipper length and weight were strongly positively associated, r = .87; within each of the three species that association was weaker, r = .47 to .70.

Make sure that second half is there. Without it your reader reads .87 as the association in one species of penguin, and that’s not what it is.
Z) Half and half — and for the half that doesn’t hold, you need the next exercise.
Is the cloud straight? Your eye says yes. You see no bend in the picture. But with what you have in hand in this exercise, you can’t prove that. You could try it like this: run a line through it and look at how much it covers. That’s R², and with one predictor that’s exactly the same number as the r² from f), to four decimals .7590. Now allow the line a bend — an extra term with flipper length squared — and it says .7753.
A good one and a half per cent extra, but that proves nothing. An extra term can only push the R² up and never down — even a term with nothing to say. (That’s not a finding but arithmetic, and you’ll meet it again in multiple regression, where a column of random numbers does exactly the same.) Whether there is a bend in it, you only see in Exercise 3.2: there a line goes through it, and it is checked how far that line is off for each stretch of the cloud. Then there turns out to be a slight bend in it after all, and it comes from the species — the same third player as with the bills.

Make a column flipper2 with flipper_length_mm^2 and run Regression → Linear Regression twice, with body_mass_g as Dependent Variable: first with only flipper_length_mm in Covariates, then with flipper_length_mm and flipper2. In Model Summary it says R² = 0.759 and then 0.775.


And no point pulls on the number all by itself. Leave out the heaviest penguin and the correlation only moves in the fourth decimal:






NoteIn JASP



Put body_mass_g < max(body_mass_g) in the filter — then exactly the heaviest animal drops out, and you don’t have to type in a weight yourself. Next to Pearson’s r it then says 0.872 instead of 0.871; to four decimals that is .8716 against .8712.


Do that in turn for all 342 and the biggest shift a single animal causes is still only .004. That’s the third decimal, and it undermines no conclusion whatsoever.






NoteIn JASP · and what can’t be done here



Doing that in turn for all 342 is not a button in JASP. The R exercise book checks it in two lines, and out comes .0042.


What hangs on it: little here, because the bend is slight. But had it been stronger, this would hold:

Stands: the three correlations within the species at g), the six species means at h), and the reasoning at i). Those describe what’s in the table, and no curved cloud changes anything about that.
Redo: not the covariance at a) and b) — that’s just a sum — but everything that expresses strength: the r at c), the r² at f) that is its square, the statement in penguin language at e) that leans on it, and the sentence at j). An r measures straightness; if the association runs curved, the number is no lie but it is a poor summary.

title: Exercise 3.1 · Correlation and the scatterplot
text:
From flipper to questionnaire
scale score · total score · the same route, a different subject
Penguins have one great advantage: you can weigh them. With people you seldom measure anything that fits on a pair of scales, and then you build your variable yourself, out of a questionnaire.
In bigfive.csv are 2634 people who rated twenty-five statements about themselves on a scale from 1 to 6. You use ten of them here: five are about neuroticism — how easily you get upset — and five about openness, the taste for new things and new ideas. One row is one person.
Ten loose answers are not yet a variable. You turn them into two numbers by taking, per person, the mean of their five answers; then everyone has one neuroticism score and one openness score, both still on that scale from 1 to 6.
One thing first. Two of the five openness statements are reversed: “Avoid difficult reading material” (O2) and “Will not probe deeply into a subject” (O5). Whoever agrees with them completely is in fact less open. You reverse those two first: 7 minus the score. A 6 becomes a 1, a 2 becomes a 5. Why 7: the two ends of the scale, 1 and 6, add up to 7. If you don’t, you add two directions together and measure something other than you think (the dataset page warns about it too). The five neuroticism statements all point the same way.
A number like that is called a scale score: the mean of the questions that belong to one scale. The book prefers to add the questions up and calls that a total score (also sum score). It’s the same idea, only with bigger numbers, and the correlation doesn’t notice — at b) and c) you check for yourself why. Both are fine, as long as you say which one you took. This exercise book averages, because a mean stays on the same 1 to 6 as the answers themselves; that way you read a score straight back as an answer to the questionnaire.
And then you walk exactly the same round as above. That’s the intention: flipper length is now openness, and weight is neuroticism, but the route is the same, line for line.






NoteIn JASP · build the two scales · JASP 0.99.0



Open bigfive.csv and make two columns in the R box (type Scale; after the name Create Column, after the line Compute column), as in the toolbox: left of the arrow the name of the column, right of it what goes in the R box.
neuroticism   ->   rowMeans(data.frame(N1, N2, N3, N4, N5))
openness       ->   rowMeans(data.frame(O1, 7 - O2, O3, O4, 7 - O5))
Copy the right-hand side exactly; you don’t have to read it. It says “give me, per person, the mean of these five”, and for openness the reversal is right in it: 7 - O2 and 7 - O5.
Mind which mean you take here: one across five columns, per person. The mean(y) block from the drag route averages one column over all rows instead — see the toolbox.
Check that you have two new columns and that they are right: put openness in Descriptives and look at Minimum and Maximum. It should say 1.2 and 6.0. If it says 1.0 and 5.8, you forgot the reversal. If it says anything else, your reversal is off (it is 7 minus the score, for both) or you’ve got hold of the wrong column.








NoteThe same route on questionnaires



Four steps, and then the sentence this chapter leads up to.
a) Ask for the mean and the standard deviation of both scales. (four numbers, with the scale they’re on)
b) Work out the covariance between openness and neuroticism. Then do it again with the row sum instead of the row mean (a column with N1 + N2 + N3 + N4 + N5, and the same for the O’s, with the same reversal). (two numbers, and say by what factor they differ and why)
c) Divide both by the standard deviations that go with them. (two numbers, and one sentence on what you recognise here from the penguins)
d) Draw the cloud, and square the correlation. (report r², and one sentence on what a cloud like that looks like compared with the one of flipper and weight)
e) Write down what you’ve found, in two sentences and in this fixed form:

Within these n people: … (r = …). Whether that also holds beyond these n, you don’t know yet.

(fill in the n, the finding in plain words and the r — and leave that second sentence exactly as it stands; for the finding, more than one answer is right)








CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





a) Neuroticism: M = 3.16, SD = 1.19 scale points. Openness: M = 4.60, SD = 0.81 scale points. Both on the scale from 1 to 6 the questions were answered on — so the average participant sits just below the middle on neuroticism and clearly above it on openness.






NoteIn JASP



Descriptives, with neuroticism and openness in Variables: Mean (arithmetic) 3.163 and 4.598, Std. Deviation 1.195 and 0.806.


b) With the row means the covariance is −0.0865, with the row sums −2.1613. That differs by a factor of 25 (exactly, unrounded), and not by chance: a sum is five times a mean, and a covariance has two variables in it, so five times five. The same again as with the penguins’ kilos — you changed the unit and not the people.






NoteIn JASP



N_sum     ->   N1 + N2 + N3 + N4 + N5
O_sum     ->   O1 + (7 - O2) + O3 + O4 + (7 - O5)
cov_mean   ->   cov(neuroticism, openness)
cov_sum   ->   cov(N_sum, O_sum)
Out come −0.086 and −2.161.


c) Both −.09. That’s what you saw with the penguins too: as soon as you divide by the two standard deviations, the units drop out and it no longer matters whether you calculated in means or in sums.






NoteIn JASP



The standard deviations of the sums are in Descriptives: 5.973 for N_sum and 4.032 for O_sum.
r_mean     ->   cov(neuroticism, openness) / (sd(neuroticism) * sd(openness))
r_sum     ->   cov(N_sum, O_sum) / (sd(N_sum) * sd(O_sum))
Both −0.090.


d) r² = .01. And the cloud looks like it too: a thick, round blob without a clear direction, in which you can just about make out a faint slope. Set that beside the flipper-and-weight cloud from before — there the points lay in a tight streak. Here the two measures share barely one per cent of their differences.






NoteIn JASP



Regression → Correlation with openness and neuroticism, Scatter plots on. Next to Pearson’s r it says −0.090; square that yourself to .01.


That the points seem to fall into small blocks is no error: a mean of five whole numbers can only take a limited number of values, so many people land on exactly the same spot.
e) For example:

Within these 2634 people: whoever scores higher on openness scores slightly lower on neuroticism (r = −.09). Whether that also holds beyond these 2634, you don’t know yet.

That second sentence is no hedge and no modesty. Everything you’ve worked out in this chapter — the covariance, the correlation, the r² — describes the people in front of you, and nobody else. What it takes to make that step outwards is what the next movement is about.
