title: Exercise 3.1 · Correlation and the scatterplot
text:
Exam-style questions
covariance versus correlation · third player · r²
These six have the form an exam would ask this topic in: four options, and exactly one is the best — the other three may well be true and still not be the best answer. Only question 2 needs any arithmetic, and only roughly at that.






NoteExam-style questions



1. A researcher reports about these 342 penguins that the covariance between flipper length and weight is 9824.42, and adds: “that is a strong association.” Which criticism of that sentence is the best?

The number is right, but he should first have found out whether the association also holds beyond these 342 animals.
Wrong, because 9824.42 lies outside the range from −1 to +1.
The covariance does give the direction and not the strength: put the weight in kilos and it says 9.8244, while nothing about the animals has changed.
Wrong, because the association between the flipper length and the weight of 342 animals can’t be summed up in one number.

2. The covariance between flipper length and weight is 9824.42 millimetre-grams, and the two standard deviations are 14.06 millimetres and 801.95 grams — both rounded to two decimals. What is the correlation between flipper length and weight? You don’t need to calculate precisely: two of the four drop out as soon as you know where a correlation can lie.

.76
.87
12.25
698.75

3. Across all 342 penguins the correlation between bill length and bill depth is r = −.24. Within Adelie it is +.39, within Chinstrap +.65 and within Gentoo +.64. Which statement is the best?

In penguins a longer bill goes with a shallower bill; the three species on their own are too small to count against that −.24.
One of the four numbers must have been worked out wrongly — correlations with opposite signs can’t both be about the same animals.
Within each species the association does hold, so that −.24 is an error in the file.
The minus sign comes from the difference between the species and not from an association between bill length and bill depth.

4. Square the correlation between flipper length and weight and it says r² = .76. What does that .76 say?

A good three quarters of the differences in weight runs along with flipper length; why is not part of it.
Of the 342 penguins, 76 per cent lie on or close to the line.
Flipper length explains 76 per cent of a penguin’s weight.
The association between flipper length and weight is 76 per cent of what it could be at most.

5. Between flipper length and weight, the correlation across all 342 penguins is higher than within each species on its own. With the bills something else happened: there the sign flipped. Where does the difference lie?

With the flippers the three species are about the same size, with the bills they aren’t.
With the bills you measure two things on the same body part, and then the two measures work against each other.
With the bills the difference between the species lies across the association within one species; with the flippers it lies in the same direction.
With the flippers the association is so strong that the sign can no longer flip.

6. With the 2634 completed questionnaires you turn five answers into one score. Take the row mean per person and the covariance between openness and neuroticism is −0.0865; take the row sum and it is −2.1613. What happens to the correlation between those two?

It becomes 25 times as big, just like the covariance.
It stays −.09, because dividing by the two standard deviations takes the unit out.
It becomes 5 times as big, because a sum of five items is five times a mean.
You can’t say without the two standard deviations as well.









CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





1 c · 2 b · 3 d · 4 a · 5 c · 6 b
Below, for each question, is why — and why the other three options are tempting. If you got one right, you can skip it.
1. c. This is the kilo test from Your turn, now as a choice: the same bunch of animals, a different number, only because you weigh in kilos. a is true and answers a different question — whether the association holds beyond these 342 animals you indeed don’t know, but the criticism is about the word strong and not about the step outwards. b has the right range for the wrong measure: −1 to +1 is the range of the correlation, and it’s precisely the covariance that has no such range. d is the safe reflex: one number may sum up an association; that’s exactly what the correlation exists for.
2. b. Dividing by the two standard deviations: 9824.42 / (14.06 × 801.95) = .87. And you didn’t need to work it out: a correlation lies between −1 and +1, so c and d drop out at once. c is what you get if you divide only by the standard deviation of weight: 9824.42 / 801.95 = 12.25. d is the other half of that same mistake, only by the standard deviation of flipper length: 9824.42 / 14.06 = 698.75. That both fall so far outside the range is the clue: a division is missing. That leaves a, and that’s r² — the square, not the correlation itself.
3. d. The Gentoos have long, shallow bills and the Adelies short, deep ones; that species difference tilts the whole cloud downwards. a takes the number across the whole heap as the statement about a penguin, and that’s exactly the sentence this exercise forbids. b is the reaction where you blame yourself: all four numbers are right, they’re just about different heaps. c has the right half and the wrong conclusion — the −.24 is properly worked out and no error; it sums up something other than you thought.
4. a. Bookkeeping: which part of the differences the two measures share, not why. b confuses a share of the differences with a share of the animals; r² says nothing about how many penguins lie close by. c is the most tempting, and it’s one word short: it’s about the differences in weight and not about the weight. A penguin of 4200 grams is not 76 per cent flipper length. d makes r² a percentage of the maximum; that would mean r = .87 and r² = .76 are two ways of saying the same thing, and then you’d only have needed one.
5. c. Same third player, two outcomes: if the species difference lies across the association within a species, the sign flips; if it lies along it, the association across everything becomes stronger than within one species. a can be checked and isn’t true: the three species are 151, 68 and 123 animals, with the flippers just as much as with the bills. b sounds like a geometric argument but says nothing — within each species a longer bill does go with a deeper one. d makes strength a lock on the sign; the bills show that a species difference can turn a sign round however strong the association within the species.
6. b. The correlation stays −.09. A sum is five times a mean, and that sits on top of the fraction and underneath, so it cancels — the same law as with the penguins’ kilos. a carries the factor of 25 from the covariance over to the correlation, and that’s precisely what the correlation does not do. c has the right number for the wrong measure: five times holds for one variable, and a covariance has two in it, so five times five. d is too modest — you don’t need to know the standard deviations to know that they shift along in proportion.
Every number in these six questions you worked out yourself earlier on this page. The only new ones are the wrong distractors — and those are all written out above as divisions, so you can check them without having to believe them.




◠ Same shape in the book
Here: one number for the association, and the cloud that gives away what the number keeps quiet.

There it starts with the cloud, not with the number — and the straight line only comes once you’ve seen everyone who is in the cloud.

section: No penguin weighs exactly the mean
text:
No penguin weighs exactly the mean
mean · why nobody sits exactly in the middle
Somewhere on a bare rock off Antarctica stands a set of scales, and around it shuffle 342 penguins who never asked for this.1 One by one they are picked up, set on the scales, and let go again. Each time, someone writes down one number. Weight, in grams. Nothing more: 342 animals, 342 numbers.
Add up those 342 numbers, divide by 342, and out comes something tidy: 4202 grams. There you have it, the average penguin: 4.2 kilos. Only — I have been through the list, and on that whole rock there is not a single penguin that weighs 4202 grams. Not one. The average penguin is not among them.
That itches. One number that sums up 342 animals and belongs to none of them — what does a number like that actually tell you? And, perhaps more exciting: what does it leave out? Come along for a moment; we’re going to open that number up.

text:
Work out the mean in JASP
mean · standard deviation · median






NoteFirst as in the book — the twelve stones · JASP 0.99.0




Open stones.csv and click Descriptives.
Drag shine to Variables.
Make sure that under Statistics Mean (arithmetic), Std. deviation and Median are ticked (the first two are on already).

The table now reads M = 50.00, SD = 21.74 and a median of 50.


Twelve stones, the same three numbers as in the book. The mean is 50 and the median is 50 too — for these twelve, the two coincide.
But where does that 21.74 come from? In the book the answer stands as a table, at the sum of squares: for each stone the deviation from the mean, that deviation squared, and at the bottom the sum of each column. Build that table here yourself. Two columns added, two sums, and you can lay your own table next to the one in the book.






NoteThe table from the book, built yourself · JASP 0.99.0




Stay in stones.csv. In the data view, click the + to the right of the last column (Add computed column), name the column deviation, choose type Scale and the R icon, and click Create Column. Type shine - mean(shine): the shine minus the mean. Click Compute column. What you type there is a line of R. You don’t need to know that language; copying it exactly is enough. The steps are also in the toolbox.
One more column like that: square, with deviation^2. In the data view your two columns now stand next to shine: that is your table.
Descriptives: drag deviation and square to Variables, and under Statistics tick Sum.

Under Sum you now read 0 for deviation and 5200 for square (JASP puts zeros after the point; the number is the same). The last two steps you do on your calculator: 5200 / 11 = 472.73, and the square root of that is 21.74.


Lay your table next to the one in the book, beside the shine columns on the right. Anna stands at −30 and 900, Kees at −20 and 400: the same numbers. (The book puts a plus in front of the positive deviations, your program does not; the number is the same.) The sum of the deviations is 0, not roughly but exactly. The sum of the squares is 5200: the sum of squares. Divide that by eleven, twelve stones minus one, and you have the variance. The book shows why it is minus one, with three envelopes; here all you have to do is divide. Take the square root of that, and there it is: 21.74, the standard deviation you just got. Behind that one number is nothing but this table.
Now you — with the penguins you already looked at in Exercise 0.1. So you know the data; the move is new. Watch what happens to that mean and that median once the heap stops being so well-behaved.
Bring in the penguins and have three numbers worked out: the mean, the standard deviation and the median of the weight.






NoteIn JASP · give it a tug · JASP 0.99.0




Open penguins.csv in JASP (menu top left → Open).
Click Descriptives at the top.
Drag body_mass_g to the Variables box.
Open the Statistics section and make sure that Mean (arithmetic), Std. deviation and Median are ticked (the first two are on already). The table appears on the right and recalculates as you go.



Three numbers. Read them one at a time:

Mean: M = 4202. The balance point. Think of all the weights as marbles on a long plank: put your finger under 4202 and the plank sits level. The “middle” — but the middle the weight pivots around.
Standard deviation: SD = 802. The answer to the question that comes straight after the middle: and how far around it do they lie? Something like the average distance to the middle: a penguin here typically sits 800 grams or so from the mean — some much closer, some much further. (For the purist: the formula squares those distances first and takes the square root afterwards, as you just did with the stones. You can simply keep the reading intuition “typical distance to the mean”.)
Median = 4050. The middle penguin: put all 342 in a row from light to heavy and see who stands halfway. Hang on — that one sits a fair bit lower than the mean. Hold on to that itch; it comes back in a moment.







NoteThe strict reading — average distance or standard deviation?





Fair is fair: “the average distance to the middle” is not exactly what a standard deviation is. In this book I mostly choose that cosy, slightly wrong reading anyway, because it works. Here, just this once, you see how things really stand.
Take your table of the twelve stones. In the deviation column, strip off the minus signs and add everything up: 220. Divide by twelve, so simply averaging: 220 / 12 = 18.33. That is the average distance to the middle. The standard deviation of the shine was 21.74: a different number, and a bigger one.
That is mostly the square’s doing. Anna lies three times as far from the middle as Hans, 30 against 10, but in the square column she counts nine times as heavily, 900 against 100. That is how the stones far from the middle pull the standard deviation up. A small part comes from dividing by eleven instead of twelve: divide the 5200 by twelve as well and take the root, and you land on 20.82, still a good way above the 18.33. With or without that minus one, the standard deviation never comes out below the plain average distance.
A report always gives the standard deviation. And if someone asks what that number is, you may say it the cosy way, with one thing added: roughly the typical distance to the middle, but by way of the squares, and so a little bigger.



But there is another column in the file: species. Three species of penguin walk that rock — Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo. Work out the mean per species, and throw the weights into a picture as well.






NoteIn JASP · per species




In the same Descriptives analysis, open the Basic Plots section and tick Distribution plots — there are all 342 weights in one picture.
Now drag species to the Split box: the table splits into three columns, one per species, and you read the three means straight off. (The picture splits along with it; if you want the one big hill back, take species out of Split for a moment.)



And there, the one number comes apart. Adelie: M = 3701. Chinstrap: M = 3733. Gentoo: M = 5076. Two species sitting close together around 3.7 kilos — and one species hanging a good kilo above them. The picture says the same thing in shape: not a neat hill with one top, but a hill with a thick shoulder on the right. That shoulder is the Gentoos.

title: Exercise 1.1 · The mean and the standard deviation
section: What 4202 grams does and does not tell you
text:
What 4202 grams does and does not tell you
M and SD together · outliers · what one number leaves unsaid
Back to 4202. What is that number still worth?
More than you might think — and less. First the gain. M says where the middle is, and SD says how widely the animals live around it. Those two together are already half a distribution: “mean 4202, typically 800 or so either side” tells you that a penguin of 3500 or of 4900 grams is perfectly ordinary here (within one SD of the middle), and that the heaviest on the rock — 6300 grams — is a hefty outlier. Whoever reports only the mean gives you a place without an outline; the SD is the outline.
Then the loss. That one mean, 4202, mixes three species together. Two species live around 3700, one around 5076 — and 4202 is the middle of none of the three: for the two light species it is a heavy penguin, for the Gentoos a light one. The average penguin does not exist, and now you can see why not: it is not a typical animal, it is the balance point of a mixed crowd. (That nobody weighs exactly 4202 grams says little in itself: the scales on the rock weigh in steps of 25 grams, so 4202 can’t even appear on them.)
And look what that mixing does to the SD. Within one species the spread is much smaller — Adelie 459, Chinstrap 384, Gentoo 504 — but across everything it was 802. That difference is not extra individual variation: it is the difference between the species, dressed up as spread. One number for the middle hides three middles; one number for the spread counts the distance between groups as if it were ordinary wobble.
Now for the median’s itch. 4050 against 4202: the mean lies higher, because the heavy Gentoo shoulder on the right pulls the balance point towards itself — the median couldn’t care less about shoulders and outliers, it only counts who stands halfway along the row. When mean and median drift apart, that is a signal: this distribution is skewed, or made of pieces. That is what the exercise on the shape of distributions is about; and whether such a difference between groups is real or could also have been chance, that we will shuffle later. For now, the signal will do.
In plain words, one sentence: these 342 penguins weigh about 4.2 kilos on average, with a typical deviation of a little over 800 grams — but that mean mixes three species that each live around a middle of their own.
And that is, from now on, how you read every mean you come across — “the average Dutchman”, “the average income”, “the average patient”. Two questions to go with it, always: how far around it do they lie? (ask for the SD) and who exactly is in that mean? (ask for the groups). A mean without those two answers is an address without a town.

text:
From belly to bill
the same two measures on a second variable
Your turn — from belly to bill. penguins.csv also holds the column bill_length_mm (in mm). The same two measures, a different variable — and a heap that lies just a little differently from the one for weight.
But first, one column that is not complete. Until now every penguin had a weight and a bill. In nitrogen the measurement is missing for a few animals. That number is not an amount of nitrogen but a measure of what a penguin ate, read from its blood (see what each column means). That is where question a) starts.
First set up the analysis below, then answer the questions. In brackets, each time, is what belongs in a complete answer, so you can check yourself without opening our answer. Where it says more than one answer is right, the wording is up to you — for the rest, the answer is fixed. The last question is called Z) on purpose, and not m): the assumptions always come last, and the odd letter says “and also, every time, this one”.






NoteIn JASP · first the gaps, then the bills




In the same Descriptives analysis, drag nitrogen to the Variables box (and body_mass_g out). To check: Valid 330, Missing 12, M = 8.73.
What is switched on? JASP leaves a penguin without a measurement out by itself and carries on with the rest. It does say so, in the Missing row, but only whoever looks there sees it. The number you computed with is under Valid, and that is not the number of rows in your file.
Then put bill_length_mm in the Variables box (and nitrogen out). Under Statistics, Mean (arithmetic), Std. deviation and Median are already on. To check: M = 43.92, SD = 5.46, Mdn = 44.45. Under Basic Plots, Distribution plots is still on: there is the whole heap of bill lengths.
Drag species to the Split box: the same three measures, now per species in a column of its own. Put nitrogen in alongside for a moment, and the Missing row also shows you how many gaps each species has. Then take species out of Split again.
For question e) you make a column that says, for each penguin, whether its bill lies within one standard deviation. In the data view, click the + to the right of the last column (Add computed column), name the column inside, choose the R icon, click Create Column and type abs(bill_length_mm - mean(bill_length_mm)) <= sd(bill_length_mm). Copy it exactly; you don’t have to read it. For each penguin it asks: is this bill no further from the mean than one standard deviation? Click Compute column, put inside under Variables and tick Frequency tables. To check: true 204 times.









NoteYour turn



a) Work out the mean of nitrogen. How many penguins are you computing with then, and why isn’t that 342? (two numbers, and one sentence)
b) Compute the mean and the standard deviation of the bill length. (two numbers to two decimals, with their unit)
c) Say in one sentence what that mean says about the bills. (about bills — a number is allowed, as long as its unit is there)
d) And what does that standard deviation say? (one sentence, with the word distance in it)
e) Count how many penguins have a bill that lies within one standard deviation of the mean, so between 43.92 − 5.46 and 43.92 + 5.46 mm. What percentage of the 342 is that? For a heap shaped like a bell (one hill, thick in the middle) a rule of thumb says about 68% lie there. Does that hold here, and why or why not? (a count, a percentage, and one sentence about the shape of the heap in your picture)
f) Look up the median. Does it lie above or below the mean? (one number, and which way)
g) For weight the median was 4050 and the mean 4201.75. For both variables, subtract the median from the mean. (two numbers, and one sentence about what the sign tells you)
h) Is that 5.46 mm a lot, then? For both variables, divide the standard deviation by its own mean — why may you lay those two side by side, and not the bare 5.46 mm and 801.95 g? (two percentages, and one sentence)
i) Work out the mean per species. (three numbers, with their n)
j) For weight, Adelie and Chinstrap lay close together and Gentoo hung a good kilo above them. Which two lie together here? (two species names, and one sentence)
k) Work out the standard deviation per species and lay those three next to the 5.46 of all 342 together. (three numbers, and one sentence about where the difference comes from)
l) Write a conclusion about what it all means, in no more than five sentences. (about penguins and species — a number is allowed, as long as its unit is there; more than one answer is right)
Z) Can you believe everything above? Check:

are measurements missing, and would they shift your mean and spread?
does every row measure the same thing — the same bill, the same unit?
does that one mean describe one heap, or three heaps mixed together?

And then the question that always belongs at the end: if something goes wrong, which answers above do you redo, and which may stand?








CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





a) M = 8.73 ‰, computed on 330 of the 342 penguins. For twelve animals the nitrogen measurement is missing (too little blood, no blood sample, or a result that never came back from the lab), and those twelve cannot take part. So always put the n with it: “mean 8.73” without n hides the fact that twelve penguins are missing. The box What is switched on? above tells you whether your program refuses at such a gap or quietly carries on computing.
b) M = 43.92 mm and SD = 5.46 mm.
c) The balance point of all 342 bills lies at almost 44 millimetres. And just as with weight, nobody lives there: rounded to one decimal, not a single penguin has a bill of 43.9 mm.
d) A bill here lies typically some 5.5 mm from that balance point — the average distance to the middle, roughly.
e) 204 of the 342 penguins, or 59.6%: a good way below the 68%. The rule of thumb holds for a bell, and the bills are not a bell. In your picture you see two humps: the Adelies with short bills, around 39 mm, and the Chinstraps and Gentoos with long ones, around 48 mm. The mean of 43.92 falls in the thin stretch between them. So right around that middle there are fewer penguins than in a bell, and then fewer fall within one standard deviation too. It is the shape that breaks the 68%: two humps with a thin middle. The bell shape itself you will meet further on in the book.
f) The median is 44.45 mm and so lies above the mean.
g) Weight: 4201.75 − 4050 = +151.75 grams. Bill: 43.92 − 44.45 = −0.53 mm. The sign flips, and that is the news. For weight, the heavy Gentoo shoulder pulled the balance point to the right, above the middle penguin; for the bills the heap leans a touch the other way. The same 342 animals, two variables, two shapes.
h) Bill: 5.46 / 43.92 = 12.4%. Weight: 801.95 / 4201.75 = 19.1%. Millimetres and grams cannot be laid side by side — 5.46 against 801.95 only says that a gram is smaller than a millimetre is big. Divide each spread by its own middle and the unit drops out above and below the fraction bar, leaving you a bare number that you may compare. And then it turns out the weight spreads, relatively, a good one and a half times as widely as the bill.
i) Adelie M = 38.79 (n = 151), Chinstrap M = 48.83 (n = 68), Gentoo M = 47.50 (n = 123).
j) Chinstrap and Gentoo lie close together here, 48.83 against 47.50; Adelie stands apart, nine to ten millimetres below. For weight the grouping was exactly the other way round — there Adelie and Chinstrap belonged together and Gentoo stood alone. So which species “belong together” depends on what you measure, and not on the species.
k) Adelie 2.66, Chinstrap 3.34, Gentoo 3.08 — all three well below the 5.46 of the whole rock. You saw the same thing happen with weight: within a species the spread is small, and what you measure on top of that, across the whole rock, is no longer individual difference but the difference between the species, dressed up as spread.
l) More than one answer is right; which five sentences you choose is up to you. Numbers are allowed — what matters is that every number says what it measures, because “43.92” is nothing and “43.92 millimetres of bill” is a penguin. For example: the 342 penguins have a bill of almost 44 millimetres on average, with a typical deviation of about five and a half millimetres. That one mean describes no penguin at all, because three species are mixed together: the Adelies have clearly shorter bills than the Chinstraps and the Gentoos, which hardly differ from each other. Within a species the spread is about three millimetres — well below the five and a half of the whole rock. So whoever knows the species already knows a good deal about how long the bill is.
Z) Yes — and mind why, because the answer here is different from the one you will get later. In this exercise nothing was tested and nothing was estimated: you have only described these 342 penguins. So almost nowhere does a distributional assumption sit under your answers. The only one is the 68% at e), and you already saw that one go down: that rule belongs to a bell, and the bills are not one. What fell there is the expectation of 68%; your count of 204 simply stands.
What can fall over here is the data itself.

Stands, as long as the n is there: a). That mean is about 330 penguins, not 342. Then also look at where the gaps are: count them per species (the box at the top shows how). Ten of the twelve are among the Adelies, while that species is not even half the rock (151 of the 342). So the mean of the 330 leans a little less on Adelies than that of all 342 would have. How much difference that makes, you don’t know: those twelve measurements you simply don’t have.
Stands: d) up to and including k). They are descriptions of exactly these 342 animals, and they stay right as long as the measurements are right. If a row were added or one dropped out, they would all shift along — not because an assumption breaks, but because you are describing something else.
Stands, with a warning attached: b), and with it c) and l). The number 43.92 is simply right. But the sentence “the average penguin has a bill of 43.9 mm” is misleading, and the third question above is exactly why: that mean mixes three species. The number answers a different question from the one you thought you were asking.

And that is the habit this exercise wants to send you off with: before you read out a mean, first check whether it is about one heap. Later, once there is testing, a second list joins this one — the answers you have to redo.

Write it up like a researcher
reporting · M and SD in one sentence · italics






NoteReporting



Reporting sounds like something with thick handbooks and cold sweat, but it is a shopping list in sentence form: what did you study, where did it lie, how spread out — done. Look:

The 342 penguins in the sample weighed over four kilos on average (M = 4201.75 g, SD = 801.95).

That’s it. The whole report — and the sentence stands on its own feet: who got weighed, what was measured, and in brackets the two numbers. Almost too simple for words, and that is exactly the nice part: it is allowed to be this simple. Two small conventions are already creeping in: only the symbols M and SD are in italics — the ordinary words stay upright — and decimals get a point (43.9, not a comma).
Your turn: write a self-standing sentence like that for the bill length (M = 43.92, SD = 5.46). Reading it out loud is allowed. You get used to it quickly, promise.

title: Exercise 1.1 · The mean and the standard deviation
text:
Exam-style questions
what an SD measures · mean against median · relative spread · reporting with n
Above were the open questions; here are the same topics once more, in the form an exam would ask them in. Six of them, four options, and exactly one is the best — the other three may well be true and still not the best answer. Calculating is only needed for question 1, and there the options lie far enough apart to estimate; you don’t need an exact number.






NoteExam-style questions



1. “Within one standard deviation of the mean” means: between M − SD and M + SD. The mean weight is M = 4201.75 grams and the standard deviation SD = 801.95 grams. Where do those two limits lie?

2597.85 and 5805.66 grams
2700 and 6300 grams
3399.80 and 5003.70 grams
3800.78 and 4602.73 grams

2. The mean weight on the rock is 4202 grams, and not a single penguin weighs exactly that. Why does this mean not describe an ordinary penguin?

Because not a single penguin weighs exactly 4202 grams: a mean that nobody weighs describes nobody.
The weights are right-skewed, and then the mean lies beside the hump.
The mean is the balance point of three species that each live around a middle of their own: for the two light species 4202 is heavy, for the Gentoos it is light.
The heaviest penguin, at 6300 grams, lifts the mean away from the other animals.

3. For weight the mean lies at 4201.75 grams and the median at 4050 grams. Which statement about those two is the best?

The mean lies higher because the heavy Gentoos pull the balance point towards themselves; the median only counts who stands halfway along the row.
The median is the better measure here, because with a mixed heap you may not use the mean.
The mean is the better measure here, because it uses all 342 animals and the median throws information away.
That the two lie 151.75 grams apart points to measurement errors in the weights.

4. Weight spreads with SD = 801.95 grams, bill length with SD = 5.46 mm. You want to know which of the two spreads relatively more widely. Which calculation goes with that question?

801.95 − 5.46, the difference between the two standard deviations.
801.95 / 5.46, the one standard deviation divided by the other.
Simply lay the two side by side; weight clearly spreads more widely.
Divide each standard deviation by its own mean, and lay those two bare numbers side by side.

5. Of the 342 penguins, 204 (59.6%) have a bill within one standard deviation of the mean. For a heap shaped like a bell, a rule of thumb says about 68% lie there. Why does this heap not get there?

342 penguins is too few; with more animals that 68% does turn up.
The heap has two humps with a thin middle, so right around the mean there are fewer animals than in a bell.
The mean, at 43.92 mm, lies below the median of 44.45 mm, and a difference like that always pushes the count below the 68%.
The rule of thumb belongs to the median and not to the mean.

6. The mean of nitrogen is 8.73 ‰, and for twelve of the 342 penguins that measurement is missing. Which report is the best?

M = 8.73 ‰ (n = 342) — that is how many penguins are in the file.
You may not report this mean, because JASP left out the twelve penguins without a measurement and computed over the rest.
M = 8.73 ‰ (n = 330) — with twelve missing measurements you computed over 330 animals.
Set the twelve gaps to zero, then you compute over all 342 and hide nothing.









CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





1 c · 2 c · 3 a · 4 d · 5 b · 6 c
Below, for each question, is why — and why the other three options are tempting. If you got one right, you can skip it.
1. c. The SD taken off once and added on once: 3399.80 and 5003.70 grams. In between lives the perfectly ordinary middle of the rock — a penguin of 5000 grams still just fits inside. a works with two standard deviations instead of one. b is the lightest and the heaviest penguin; that is the range, and it hangs on two animals. d halves the SD and shares it out over the two sides, as if “within one SD” meant that the whole band is one SD wide — it is two.
2. c. Two species live around 3700 grams and one around 5076, and 4202 is an ordinary weight for none of the three. a is the hook of this exercise, and it proves less than it seems: the scales on the rock weigh in steps of 25 grams — all 342 weights are a multiple of 25 — so a weight like 4202 cannot even be there. There are plenty of penguins around 4200: five weigh exactly 4200, thirty from 4100 up to and including 4300. That nobody weighs exactly the mean says something about the scales; that the mean fits none of the species says something about the penguins — and an exam asks about that difference. b names the shape and not the cause. That the heap leans to the right, this exercise says itself — but that explains why the mean lies higher than the median, not why it fits none of the species. The two are easily confused: skewness shifts the mean up, the mixing of species puts it between the species. d makes one animal of what is a whole group — take that 6300 away and the mean shifts a few grams; take the Gentoos away and it shifts hundreds of grams.
3. a. The median counts places in the row, the mean weighs the distances too, and so the heavy Gentoo shoulder pulls only on the mean. b picks the same middle on the strength of a ban that does not exist: a mean is allowed with a mixed heap, it just answers a different question — if you want to know how much these 342 animals weigh together, the mean is exactly right. c is right in what it claims (the mean really does use all 342) and draws the wrong conclusion; “more animals taken in” is not the same as “better middle”. d invents a cause that isn’t there: the two middles drift apart because the heap is skewed or made of pieces, not because the weighing was sloppy.
4. d. Divide each spread by its own mean and the unit drops out above and below the fraction bar, leaving you two bare numbers: 12.4% for the bill and 19.1% for the weight. Those you may compare. a subtracts grams from millimetres, and then the result is neither. b is the most tempting, because a ratio already feels unit-free — but above the bar are grams and below it millimetres, and those do not cancel each other out. c draws the very conclusion the question warns against: 801.95 is only a bigger number, not a wider spread.
5. b. Your histogram shows two humps — the Adelies around 39 mm, the Chinstraps and Gentoos around 48 — with the mean of 43.92 in the thin stretch between them. So right around that middle there are fewer animals than in a bell, and then fewer fall within one standard deviation too. It is the shape that breaks the rule of thumb. a points at the sample size, and that is exactly what plays no part here: the rule of thumb hangs on the shape of the heap, not on how many animals are in it. c builds, on two correct numbers, a cause that isn’t there. That the two middles lie apart is indeed a sign that the heap is not a bell — at g) that is called “the news”, and so it is. But that sign is in the direction, not in the size: 0.53 mm on a spread of 5.46 mm is too small to tell which way the count goes, let alone “always”. d moves the rule over to the median; the rule of thumb was written with the mean and the standard deviation.
6. c. The n belongs with it, and the n is 330. “Mean 8.73” without n hides the fact that twelve penguins are missing. a gives the number of rows in the file instead of the number of animals computed with, and here those are two different numbers — that is the whole trap of a column with gaps. b confuses what JASP does with what you may do: that it leaves out the twelve is stated plainly in the Missing row, and what remains is a perfectly reportable mean over the animals that are there. d is the most dangerous of the three, because it looks like honesty: zero is not a missing measurement but a measured zero, and twelve zeros added in pull the mean down to a number that describes no penguin at all.
If you want to see for yourself where the numbers from question 1 come from: you work out the right two on your calculator from the numbers in the question, 4201.75 − 801.95 = 3399.80 and 4201.75 + 801.95 = 5003.70. The lightest and the heaviest penguin of option b are in Descriptives under Minimum and Maximum. Options a and d were computed on the unrounded mean and the unrounded standard deviation; if you check them with the rounded numbers from the question, the last digit can differ by a hundredth. That is rounding, not a different sum.

First movement · Difference under the microscope
Maybe you have never opened a statistics program before. Then this exercise book begins exactly where it should, because that is where everyone once began: with an empty screen and a slight doubt about whether this is really for you. It is for you. We do one download and one tour of the window, without hurrying, and after that you are ready. No maths yet, no buttons you have to remember — just getting to know the place where we will be working in the exercises to come.
The place is called JASP. It is a program that works out the statistics for you, made at the University of Amsterdam, and it is completely free — no trial period, no account, no paywall that turns up after a month. You install it once and then it is yours.

title: Exercise 0.0 · Installing & setting up
text:
Getting and installing JASP
Go to jasp-stats.org/download. You see a page with a big button and a choice between operating systems. Pick yours. This exercise book is written for JASP 0.99.0; if you already have an older JASP, get this one instead, because a few buttons are different in an older version.

Mac — download the file (it ends in .dmg), double-click it, and drag the JASP icon into your Applications folder. Done. The first time you open JASP, the Mac may ask whether you really want to open it because it came from the internet — you can safely confirm that.
Windows — download the installation file (it ends in .msi), double-click, and click your way through the installation window (just Next each time). When it is done, JASP is in your Start menu.

That is all there is to it. Now go and open JASP. You see a mostly empty window, with a bar full of buttons along the top. A moment’s fright, maybe, but it is really not that bad — there are only three places that matter, and we walk through them together now.

title: Exercise 0.0 · Installing & setting up
text:
A tour of the window



The JASP window.


Three places, and that is all you need to begin with. From left to right:

Top left: the menu ≡ — this is where you open your data. Those three stripes stacked on top of each other are your way in to your files. Click them, choose Open → Computer, and find the data file that goes with an exercise (for us, always a .csv file that you download). JASP first shows a preview (Data Preview); click Load, and then JASP lays your data out as a neat table: every column a variable, every row a case.
Along the top: the ribbon — this is where you choose an analysis. The bar of buttons — Descriptives, T-Tests, ANOVA, Regression, Frequencies and a few more — is the list of everything JASP can work out. You click the button that fits your question and, in the small menu that drops down, choose the analysis — under Descriptives that is nearly always Descriptive Statistics. Then a panel opens up in which you drag your variables into the correct boxes. In every exercise I point you to exactly the button you need, so you don’t have to remember anything now.
On the right: the results panel — this is where your results appear. As soon as you drag a variable into the correct box, JASP calculates live, as you go, and puts the table or graph on the right straight away. No ‘calculate’ button, no waiting: you see your answer while you click. Change something on the left, and the result on the right changes with it, by itself.

One more thing to recognise: above every column in your data table sits a small icon. It tells you the measurement level of that column — whether it holds separate categories (nominal), an order (ordinal), or numbers you really calculate with (scale). If such an icon is ever wrong, you click it and choose the right one. We come back to this in the exercises; for now it is enough that you know that they are there and what they mean.

One small convention
One convention about numbers to keep in mind: the decimal mark is a point, not a comma. So 5.03, not 5,03. The data files for this exercise book all use points. And should you ever type in a number yourself, remember the point.
Also, set JASP to English, as in this book; then the buttons have the names they have here. If yours is set to another language: menu ≡ → Preferences → Interface → Choose language, and pick English (in the list it starts with en).
When you open a file, take a quick look at the preview JASP shows first (Data Preview). Under Read numbers as written in it should say en - American English, and it usually does already; if it says something else, choose that one. Then check that the numbers in the small preview table look as they do in your file, with the point in them: for the penguins, the first row says 39.1. In that preview the words stand between double quotes (""Adelie""); that is how it should be, and after loading they are gone. If it all looks right, click Load.

The left one is fatter than the right one
looking before calculating · feeling difference
Before there is any calculating, there is looking. Someone stands on a cold rock, sees two penguins waddle past and thinks: the left one is fatter than the right one. That’s all it is. No formula, no test — a glance, and the beginning of a question.
That is how the book began too: with feeling difference, long before anything got calculated. This exercise book is the other half of that story, and it runs alongside it the whole way: the book tells the story, here you do it yourself. You and JASP — and the idea is that, step by step, you get that computer to show what you could already feel.
But before you touch a single button, I want you to do something almost everyone skips: look at what data actually is. Not calculating — looking.

Look at the table in JASP
opening a file · rows and columns






NoteFirst as in the book — the twelve stones · JASP 0.99.0




Open stones.csv in JASP (menu top left → Open).
Look first in the data view, on the left: twelve rows, nine columns — it all fits on one screen.
Go along the columns: which ones hold numbers, and which hold text? That is all that is needed here.



Twelve rows, nine columns — the whole dataset fits in a single glance, and that is exactly why the book calculates with it. With real data, seeing it all in one go no longer works, and then you need tools to see what’s there.
Now you — with 342 penguins, too many rows for a single glance.
A file comes with this exercise book: penguins.csv — 342 penguins from a rock near Antarctica, really picked up, really weighed.1 Download it and just look. Nothing gets calculated here.






NoteIn JASP · just look · JASP 0.99.0




Open the file: menu (≡, top left) → Open → Computer, and browse to penguins.csv.
On the left, the data view appears, laid out like a spreadsheet: the table itself. Scroll slowly through it, from row 1 to row 342. Don’t click on anything, just look.
See the small icons in front of the column names (a ruler, some bars)? JASP has already guessed what kind of data is in each column. We’ll come back to that — for now, just notice that they are there.



What you see is a table: 342 rows, nine columns — id, species, sex, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, nitrogen and carbon. And with it the most important reading rule of this whole exercise book: one row is one penguin. Row 1 is an Adelie male with a bill (the beak) of 39.1 mm, and he weighs 3750 grams. Look in his row under nitrogen and carbon: there, nothing has been filled in, twice. A measurement is missing at that spot — no fault of yours, and no fault in the file. What those two columns are is on the dataset page. Now scroll a good way down: row 173 is a Gentoo of 5000 grams. Go on, point at them both. This bird weighs 3750 grams; that bird 5000 — a good kilo between them, two animals, one rock.
You haven’t calculated a thing yet. And still you’ve already seen something.

section: What a table is — and what it leaves out
text:
What a table is — and what it leaves out
what data is · measuring · look first, then calculate
This is data. Nothing mystical, no maths — a table. Every row a real animal (or later, in other files, a real person), and every column a question someone put to that animal: how heavy are you, how long is your bill, what species are you.
And straight away this too, because it belongs here from day one: the table is not the penguin. Row 1 says nothing about how that animal waddled across the rock, whether it let itself be picked up or protested, what the wind was doing that day. What you measure is never everything there was. A dataset is a net of numbers that tries to hold on to a piece of reality — and something always slips through. But what does stay in the net is something you can look with. That is not a loss to keep mourning; it is a beginning.
From here on, we’re going to get that table talking, a little more cleverly each time. Chapter by chapter, one technique at a time: first summarising, then drawing, then shuffling, and in the end predicting. And every time in the same order, the one you already know: look first, then calculate.

title: Exercise 0.1 · Looking at the data
text:
Exam-style questions
one row is one penguin · an empty cell · text versus number · what the first rows show
There is nothing to calculate in this exercise yet, and still an exam can already ask about it. These five have that form: four options, and exactly one is the best — the other three may well be true and still not be the best answer.






NoteExam-style questions



1. penguins.csv has 342 rows and 9 columns. What is in one row?

One measurement on one penguin.
One of the nine things that were measured on the penguins.
One penguin, with all its measurements side by side.
One of the three species of penguin.

2. For the first penguin, nothing has been filled in under nitrogen and carbon — twice. What does that mean?

A measurement is missing in those two places.
Those two measurements came out at zero.
A mistake was made when opening the file.
That penguin doesn’t belong in the dataset and should be taken out.

3. You want to know how many penguins are in the file. Where on your screen do you see that?

The number of columns in the data view.
The names at the top of the columns.
The rows you see as soon as you open the file.
The number of the last row with a penguin in it.

4. The column species holds text (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo); the column body_mass_g holds numbers (3750, 5000, …). Because of that difference, what will you later be able to do with body_mass_g and not with species?

Add the values together and so make one number out of them.
Count how often each value occurs.
Sort the rows on that column.
Nothing — you can do exactly the same with both columns.

5. You open the file and look at the first six rows: all six penguins are Adelies. What may you conclude from that?

That more than half of the penguins in the file are Adelies.
That the file is sorted by species.
Nothing about the other 336 — six rows are a peek, not a summary.
That the Chinstraps and Gentoos are in a different file.









CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





1 c · 2 a · 3 d · 4 a · 5 c
Below, for each question, is why — and why the other three options are tempting. If you got one right, you can skip it.
1. c. This is the reading rule of this whole exercise book: one row is one penguin, and the nine columns are the nine things written down about that one animal. a lies closest to it, and is the most important one to tell apart from it: one measurement sits in one cell, where a row and a column cross. Read a row as one measurement and you lose the idea that the measurements of the same animal belong together — and that idea, later on, is everything. b describes a column: nine things, nine columns. d confuses the table with a grouping; the species is one of the nine columns, not the unit a row is about.
2. a. An empty cell means: a measurement belongs here, and it isn’t here. No fault of yours, and no fault in the file. b is the most dangerous of the three, because zero is a measurement — a measured zero says “I looked and there was nothing”, and an empty cell says “I didn’t look” or “it didn’t work”. Later, that difference is the difference between a mean that is right and one that has been dragged down by made-up zeros. c looks for the cause in how the file was opened; you see the gap because it is really there. d throws away a penguin over two missing measurements, while its weight and its bill are right there and join in just fine.
3. d. JASP numbers the rows on the left of the data view, and one row is one penguin — so the number of the last row with a penguin in it, 342, is the number of animals. a counts the columns and gives 9: the number of things measured, not the number of animals. That is the same mix-up as in question 1, now on your screen. b gives the nine column names, so it does say what the file is about, and not how many. c shows a piece of the table and says nothing about the rest — see question 5.
4. a. Weights you can add up; species you can’t. Adelie plus Gentoo is nothing, and Chinstrap is not twice Adelie — the text in that column is a label, not an amount. That sounds obvious, and it is the floor under everything you are about to do: what you can do with a column depends on what is in it. b works for both — how often Adelie occurs is just as countable as how often 3750 grams occurs. c works for both too: text sorts alphabetically, numbers by size. d is the trap, because two of the four things really do work for both; adding up is precisely what sets the two columns apart.
5. c. The first rows show what is there — which columns, what kind of values, where the gaps are — and nothing about what the other 336 rows look like. If you want to know that, you scroll through the whole table, down to row 342. b is the most tempting, and it fails on one point: six rows cannot show it. You could get six Adelies in a row in a file where nothing is in order, too. That is the difference between it’s true and you’ve seen it — and here it is even nearly true, because the animals really are kept together by species: first 151 Adelies, then 123 Gentoos, then 68 Chinstraps. Grouped, then, not sorted, because alphabetically Chinstrap would be in the middle. a is a statement about all 342 on the strength of six, and that is exactly the leap this question is there to stop. It is also untrue here: 151 of the 342 waddling about are Adelies, or 44.2% — the largest group of the three, but no majority. d invents a second file; all three species are in this one.
If you want to see the numbers from these five questions again, on your own screen:

The number of penguins and the number of columns are in the data view: 342 rows, nine columns. You work out 342 − 6 = 336 yourself.
Click Descriptives, drag species to Variables and tick Frequency tables. Next to Adelie it says 151, and in the Percent column the percentage from answer 5: 44.2.
Scroll down the species column in the data view: first the Adelies, then the Gentoos, then the Chinstraps.

title: Exercise 2.1 · Median, quartiles and skewness
section: The middle that lies above the middle
text:
The middle that lies above the middle
mean · typical day · shape of the heap
New York, the summer of 1973. On a narrow island in the East River stands a measuring box that does the same thing every day: sniff, count, write down how much ozone is hanging in the air.1 Ozone at street level is the stuff smog is made of — the higher the number, the harder the city breathes. The box passes no judgement. All it does is collect a heap of numbers, a hundred and sixteen days long. And in the shape of that heap — for anyone who looks closely — sits the whole summer.
And now us. The first question anyone asks of a column like this is the one from the exercise on the mean: what is an average ozone day? Add up, divide, done: 42.1. A nice, tidy story — until you leaf through the column itself. It starts like this: 41, 36, 12, 18, 28, 23, 19, 8… mostly numbers that stay below 42, and then suddenly, further on, a day of 168. Count it: of the 116 days, only 44 come out above the mean. So the ‘average day’ is a day that most days don’t reach.
How can a middle lie above the middle? And what, then, is a typical ozone day in that summer? Come along for a moment — the answer isn’t in yet another number, but in the shape of the heap.

text:
Two middles and two pictures in JASP
mean · median · quartiles · histogram · boxplot






NoteFirst as in the book — the twelve stones · JASP 0.99.0




Descriptives, shine to Variables.
Under Statistics, tick: Median, Quartiles.
Under Customizable Plots: Boxplots.

Median 50, Q1 = 30, Q3 = 70 — the middle half lies in a band of 40 points.


The median of the shine is 50, with Q1 = 30 and Q3 = 70: the middle half of the stones sits in a band of 40 points, neatly symmetric around the middle. That’s what a boxplot looks like when nothing odd is going on.
Now you — with something you haven’t seen yet: air readings from New York. Those do lean to one side, and that is exactly when the median and the quartiles take on the work the mean fails at.
Bring the summer in and ask for two things: the middles, and a picture of the whole heap.






NoteIn JASP · give it a tug · JASP 0.99.0




Open airquality.csv in JASP (menu top left → Open).
Click Descriptives at the top.
Drag ozone to the Variables box.
Open the Statistics section and, next to Mean (arithmetic) (that one is already on), also tick Median, Quartiles and Skewness.
Open the Basic Plots section and tick Distribution plots, and under Customizable Plots the Boxplots.



There they are, two middles side by side. The mean is 42.1. The median — lay all 116 days in order and take the middle one — is 31.5. Eleven points apart — for two numbers that both claim to be ‘the middle’. Add the quartiles: a quarter of the days stay below 18, a quarter come out above 63.25; in between lives the middle half of the summer.
And then the pictures. The histogram is no neat bell but a heap leaning against the left-hand side, with a long stretch trailing off to the right — plenty of clean days, a thin wisp of smog days. The boxplot sums that same heap up in five lines: a box from 18 to 63.25 with the median line low inside that box, a short whisker downwards, a long whisker upwards, and above that two more lone dots: 135 and 168. Everything there is to see points the same way. Up.

title: Exercise 2.1 · Median, quartiles and skewness
section: Why the tail lifts the mean
text:
Why the tail lifts the mean
right-skewed · balance point · robustness · choice of middle
What you’re looking at is called a right-skewed distribution. Careful: the skew is named after the tail, not after the hump. The hump leans left, but the tail points right — towards the high end — so right-skewed. (In a histogram lying flat; in the upright boxplot that same tail points up.)
And that tail explains the riddle from the hook. The mean, you see, is a balance point: every day pulls on it, and the further a day lies from the middle, the harder it pulls. Those few smog days — seven days of 100 or higher, with 168 as the champion — hang like weights on the end of a lever and lift the mean up to 42.1. The median doesn’t do levers. It only counts who sits above and who sits below, and says, unruffled: the middle day of this summer was 31.5.
Want to feel how unruffled? Thought experiment: suppose the top day hadn’t been 168 but a disastrous 500. The mean then jumps from 42.1 to 45.0 — one single day pushes the whole ‘middle’ up three points. And the median? It stays at exactly 31.5. There is still exactly one day above it on the high side, and that is all the median cares about. That’s what statisticians call robust: unmoved by what happens in the tail.
There was a hint in the numbers from the start, by the way. The standard deviation from the exercise on the mean is 33.0 here — almost as large as the mean itself. But ozone can’t go below zero: a symmetric bell around 42 with a spread of 33 would sink through the floor on the left. So the distribution couldn’t have been symmetric at all; the skew was already blinking in the summary before we had drawn a single picture.
When does the mean mislead? Right here — with skewed heaps. And the world is full of them: incomes (a handful of millionaires lifts the ‘average income’ above what almost everyone earns), waiting times, house prices, insurance claims. Wherever a distribution does have a long tail upwards and doesn’t have one downwards, the mean lies above the median and above most people’s experience. Compare it with the penguin weight from the exercise on the mean: mean 4202 grams, median 4050 — a few per cent apart, take your pick, it hardly mattered there. Here the difference is a third of the median. Hence the rule of this exercise: look at the shape of the heap first, and only then choose your middle.
One more nuance, because ‘the mean misleads’ is also too quick a verdict. Neither middle is wrong; they answer different questions. If you want to know how much ozone the city had to cope with that summer in total, the mean is exactly right — mean times number of days is the total, tail and all. If you want to know what a typical day was, what you’ll probably be breathing tomorrow, then the median should do the talking. In plain words: “the middle summer day had 31.5 parts of ozone per billion, but a handful of smog days — up to 168 — pulled the mean up to 42.” Whoever reports only ‘a mean of 42’ tells you about the tail and keeps quiet about the summer.

NoteIn JASP · the wind




In the same Descriptives analysis, drag wind to the Variables box (and ozone out).
Under Statistics, Median and Quartiles are already on; leave Mean (arithmetic) on as well. To check: Mdn = 9.70 with Q1 = 7.40 and Q3 = 11.50.
Under Basic Plots the Distribution plots and under Customizable Plots the Boxplots are still on; leave them on.









NoteYour turn



a) Look up the median and the two quartiles of the wind. (three numbers, to two decimal places)
b) Work out the IQR. Why is that one number and not two? (one number, and one sentence)
c) Work out the mean as well and subtract the median from it. (two numbers, and which way the difference points)
d) Do that same subtraction for the ozone from this exercise. (one number, and one sentence on how the two compare)
e) How many of the 116 days lie above their own mean — for the wind, and for the ozone? (two numbers, each also as a percentage)
f) Look at the boxplot of the wind. How many lone dots stand outside it, and on which side? (one number, the side, and the values themselves)
g) At c) the wind looked almost symmetric, and yet all the dots stand on one side. Do those two contradict each other? (one sentence; whether you call 0.16 ‘almost symmetric’ is up to you, which way it points is not)
h) Look up the minimum and the maximum and set the distance between them next to the IQR. (three numbers, and one sentence on why they lie so far apart)
i) Which middle would you report for the wind, and which for the ozone? (two choices, with one sentence per choice)
j) Put the rule of thumb of this exercise into your own words. (one sentence, with the word shape in it; more than one answer is right)
k) Write a conclusion about what it all means, in no more than five sentences. (about the summer of 1973 — a number is allowed, as long as the unit is next to it; more than one answer is right)
Z) Can you believe everything above? Check:

are there readings missing in this column, and what does your program do then?
does every day measure the same thing — the same box, the same unit?
is this one heap, or are there seasons running through it?

And then the question that always belongs at the end: if something goes wrong, which answers above do you redo, and which may stand?








CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





a) Mdn = 9.70, with Q1 = 7.40 and Q3 = 11.50. So the middle half of the summer days lives between a little over seven and eleven and a half miles per hour.
b) IQR = 11.50 − 7.40 = 4.10. It’s one number because it isn’t the box itself but its width — Q1 and Q3 tell you where the box lies, the IQR tells you how wide it is. That distinction is worth holding on to: two summers can have the same IQR and still lie somewhere else entirely.
c) M = 9.86, and 9.86 − 9.70 = 0.16. So the mean lies a fraction above the median — the same way round as with the ozone, but by sixteen hundredths of a mile per hour instead of a good ten parts per billion.
d) Ozone: 42.13 − 31.50 = 10.63. That is 65.59 times the 0.16 of the wind — divide the two rounded numbers on this line and you get 66, and that small difference is exactly why you round only at the end. The two columns come from the same file and cover the same 116 days. But those two differences are in different units — miles per hour against parts per billion — so that ‘sixty-six times’ puts apples next to oranges. If you want to lay them side by side fairly, divide each difference by the spread of its own column: for the wind that gives 0.045 and for the ozone 0.322. Those are two numbers without a unit, and those you may compare — the ozone remains a good seven times as skewed as the wind.
e) Wind: 54 of the 116 days, or 46.6% — nearly half, as it should be with a neat heap. Ozone: 44 of the 116, or 37.9%. That second number was the whole hook of this exercise: an ‘average day’ that most days don’t reach.
f) Three dots, all three at the top: 18.4, 20.1 and 20.7 miles per hour. At the bottom there isn’t a single one, and there hardly could be — the fence there lies at 7.40 − 1.5 × 4.10 = 1.25, and the calmest day of the summer still managed 2.3. Mind the difference between those two numbers: 1.25 is the fence, and the whisker runs to the furthest day that still falls inside that fence. So the lower whisker ends here at 2.3 and not at 1.25.
g) More than one answer is right, because the question hangs on a judgement: whether you find 0.16 miles per hour ‘almost symmetric’ is up to you. The direction is not. So no — the dots and the two middles point the same way, only much more gently. The wind too leans a little to the right; that’s exactly what the 0.16 at c) was already telling you. The difference from the ozone is not a difference in direction but in degree: skewness is not a switch that’s on or off. That degree is the soft part of the answer, and that’s why an exam can’t ask for it. The direction it can — see the exam-style questions at the end.
h) Minimum 2.3, maximum 20.7, so a distance of 18.4 — a good four times the IQR of 4.10. That’s as it should be: the distance between the extremes hangs on exactly two days, and there is nothing typical about the wilder of the two. The IQR counts only the middle half and pays those two no attention at all. That’s the same robustness the median showed with the ozone.
i) For the wind it makes no difference — the two middles differ by 0.16, so by all means pick the mean, with the standard deviation beside it. For the ozone the median should do the talking, with the quartiles beside it, because there the two middles are a third apart and the mean says more about the seven smog days than about the summer.
j) More than one answer is right; there’s no prescribed wording. For example: look at the shape of the heap first, and only then choose your middle — and if the mean and the median barely differ, the shape has just told you that the choice doesn’t matter.
k) More than one answer is right. Numbers are allowed — the point is that next to every number it says what it measures, because ‘9.70’ is nothing and ‘9.70 miles per hour on the middle day’ is a summer. For example: in the summer of 1973 the wind on Roosevelt Island blew at 9.70 miles per hour on the middle day, and half of all days sat between 7.40 and 11.50 miles per hour. That heap is nearly symmetric: the mean lies 0.16 miles per hour above the middle day, on a range running from 2.3 to 20.7. Three days stuck out at 18.4, 20.1 and 20.7 miles per hour, but they barely dragged the middle along. For the ozone from the same summer the mean lay 10.63 parts per billion above the middle day — the same 116 days, two columns, two shapes.
Z) Yes, and just as in Exercise 1.1 without a distributional assumption: nothing here has been tested, only described. Each of the three questions does take a bite out of it here, though.

Stands: a) up to and including j). In the column wind not one of the 116 readings is missing, so you’re working with every day. That can’t be taken for granted here: in the column solar_r of this file, five are missing. What your program does with a gap like that — refuse, or quietly carry on — you can read in the box What is switched on? of Exercise 1.1.
Stands, with a warning attached: the median of 9.70 as ‘the typical summer day’, and with it k). These 116 days run from May to September, and that is not one homogeneous heap: per month the median lies at 11.50 (May), 11.50 (June), 7.70 (July), 8.00 (August) and 10.30 (September). So there is clearly less wind in July and August than in spring. That 9.70 is a correct number for the summer as a whole, and at the same time a day that is not particularly typical of any single month — exactly the same pitfall as the mean that mixed three penguin species.

What does not fall over is the measuring itself: it’s one box on one island, the same every day, in the same unit. That’s the dullest of the three questions and usually the most important — change what you’re measuring halfway through, and no measure of spread can help you any more.

text:
Write it up like a researcher
Mdn · IQR · reporting a skewed distribution






NoteReporting



Remember from Exercise 1.1: reporting is a shopping list in sentence form. But with a skewed heap there’s something different on the list: not M and SD, but the shape, the median and the quartiles. Look:

The ozone concentration (in ppb) on the 116 measured summer days was right-skewed (Mdn = 31.50, IQR = 45.25; the middle half of the days lay between Q1 = 18.00 and Q3 = 63.25).

That’s it. One sentence that stands on its own feet: which days, which variable, the shape, the robust middle, and in brackets the box of the boxplot — how wide it is and where it lies. Mdn is the proper abbreviation for the median. Q1 and Q3 are the lower and the upper quartile: the two edges of the box. And IQR (interquartile range) is not that box itself but its width — 63.25 − 18.00 = 45.25. In the model sentence only the symbols are in italics; the ordinary words stay upright. And do you see what’s quietly going on? By reporting the median instead of the mean, the whole shape story is already tucked away inside the sentence.
Your turn: write a sentence like that yourself for the wind, in miles per hour (Mdn = 9.70, IQR = 4.10; the middle half of the days lay between Q1 = 7.40 and Q3 = 11.50). Choose deliberately which middle you report, now that you know the shape.

title: Exercise 2.1 · Median, quartiles and skewness
text:
Exam-style questions
choice of middle · robustness · 1.5 × IQR · direction of the skew
These six have the form an exam would ask this topic in: four options, and exactly one is the best — the other three may well be true and still not the best answer. Only question 3 needs any arithmetic.






NoteExam-style questions



1. You’re reporting the ozone of these 116 days and have to choose one middle. Which description is the best?

The median, because with a skewed distribution you aren’t allowed to use the mean.
The median, because it gives the typical day, while the smog days have pulled the mean upwards.
The mean, because it uses all 116 days and the median throws information away.
It makes no difference: M = 42.13 and Mdn = 31.50 lie less than one standard deviation (SD = 32.99) apart.

2. In the boxplot of the wind there are three lone dots, all three at the top, and the mean lies 0.16 miles per hour above the median. Which statement about the shape of the wind heap is the best?

The wind heap is symmetric; three lone dots on one side say nothing about the shape.
The wind heap leans slightly to the right: the dots and the two middles point the same way.
The wind heap is right-skewed, because as soon as there are dots on one side a distribution is skewed.
The wind heap is left-skewed, because the median (9.70) lies below the mean (9.86).

3. For the wind, Q1 = 7.40 and Q3 = 11.50 miles per hour, so IQR = 4.10 miles per hour. A day counts as a lone point above the whisker as soon as it comes out above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Which of these four wind days is the lowest one that still lies above that?

14.9 miles per hour
16.6 miles per hour
18.4 miles per hour
20.1 miles per hour

4. In your mind, lift the top day of the ozone from 168 to 500 ppb. The mean then climbs from 42.13 to 44.99, and the median stays put at 31.50. What is the reason?

The median counts how many days lie above and below, not how far away they lie.
The median leaves days out of the calculation as soon as they come out above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
The median is calculated over the middle half of the days, so the tail doesn’t count.
The median stays put as long as there are equally many days on both sides.

5. The IQR of the ozone is 45.25 ppb and that of the wind 4.10 miles per hour. What does the IQR say about a distribution?

Where the middle half of the readings lies.
How wide the middle half of the readings is.
The difference between the highest and the lowest reading, divided by four.
How far the furthest lone point lies from the median.

6. Of the ozone you know only this: the mean is 42.13 ppb, the highest day was 168 ppb, and an ozone reading can’t go below zero. What may you conclude from that about the shape of the ozone heap, before you have drawn a single picture?

Nothing — for the shape of a distribution you need a histogram or a boxplot.
The ozone heap can’t be symmetric: a day as far below the mean as 168 is above it would come out at −83.74 ppb.
The ozone heap is symmetric, because 42.13 lies roughly midway between zero and the highest day.
The ozone heap is left-skewed, because there’s more room above the mean than below it.









CautionAnswer — open after your own attempt





1 b · 2 b · 3 c · 4 a · 5 b · 6 b
Below, for each question, is why — and why the other three options are tempting. If you got one right, you can skip it.
1. b. The median gives the typical day, and the seven days of 100 ppb or higher have pulled the mean to 42.13. a picks the same middle on the strength of a ban that doesn’t exist: a mean is allowed with a skewed heap, it just answers a different question. If you want to know how much ozone the city had to cope with that summer in total, the mean is exactly right — mean times number of days is that total. That’s the difference between wrong and a different question, and an exam asks about that difference. c is right in what it claims — the mean really does use all 116 days — and draws the wrong conclusion from it; ‘more days included’ is not the same as ‘better middle’. d tempts you with a real calculation: 10.63 really is less than 32.99. But that says nothing, because that SD of 32.99 is itself inflated by the very tail that causes the problem.
2. b. Direction: right. Degree: small. a throws the dots away while they count as a clue. c turns skewness into a switch that’s on or off, and it isn’t one — the wind leans the same way as the ozone, and a seventh as far. d has the right reason and the wrong label: the median lying below the mean is exactly what right-skewed means. That’s the confusion that names the skew after the hump instead of after the tail.
3. c. The fence lies at 11.50 + 1.5 × 4.10 = 17.65 miles per hour, and 18.4 is the lowest wind day that comes out above it. a and b are both days of hard wind that still fall inside the whisker — 14.9 and 16.6 stay below 17.65, and high here is not the same as lone point. That b lies so close is no accident: 16.6 is the highest day that still just falls inside, and that one draws the end of the line. So the whisker stops at 16.6 and not at 17.65. d is a lone point, only not the lowest of the three — the question asks for the first one that falls outside, not the worst.
4. a. The median counts places in the row, not distances. Whether the top day is 168 or 500: equally many days lie above the median, so the middle day doesn’t change. The mean does count distances, and so climbs to 44.99. b confuses robustness with crossing out: the 1.5 × IQR rule decides what gets drawn as a lone point in a boxplot, but the median throws nothing away — that 500 simply takes part, it just counts as one day and not as a far-off day. c mixes the median up with the IQR; the median uses all 116 days. (And it gives a different number: the median of only the middle half is 31.00, not 31.50.) d sounds right and can’t be: above and below the median there are by definition always equally many days — that’s what a median is, not a condition it has to meet.
5. b. The IQR is Q3 − Q1, so the width of the box. a is the answer almost everyone gives first, and it’s the position: where the middle half lies is what Q1 and Q3 tell you. Two summers can have the same IQR of 4.10 and still lie somewhere else entirely. c sounds like a quartile sum but isn’t one; the range divided by four hangs on the two extreme days, and that’s exactly what the IQR doesn’t do. d measures from the median to a lone point and so uses the tail, of all things.
6. b. In a symmetric heap, for every day above the mean there’s a day just as far below it. The top day of 168 lies 168 − 42.13 = 125.87 above the mean, so its mirror image would lie at 42.13 − 125.87 = −83.74 ppb. No such day exists: ozone stops at zero. So the heap can’t be symmetric, and you knew that before the histogram. a is the safe habit and too modest here: a floor that nature lays down is itself information about the shape. c is the most tempting, because it sounds like a test for symmetry — but work it out: the midpoint between zero and the highest day lies at 84.00 ppb, and the mean lies at 42.13 ppb, so 41.87 ppb lower. In a symmetric heap those two coincide. That they lie so far apart here points to skewness. d sniffs out the skew correctly and sticks the wrong label on it: the room is at the top, so the tail points right, and that’s called right-skewed.
If you want to see for yourself where the numbers from these six questions come from: the sums in answers 3 and 6 are written out in full above, and those you can check with your calculator. Question 4 can be done with the calculator too, and then you see straight away why the mean shifts. The mean is the sum of all 116 days, divided by 116. If one day becomes 500 − 168 = 332 ppb heavier, the mean shifts by 332 / 116 = 2.86: 42.13 + 2.86 = 44.99. The median doesn’t shift, because the middle day stays the same day.






NoteIn JASP · the wind days around the fence




Click the funnel above the data and type in the R box wind <= 17.65. Put wind in Descriptives: next to Maximum you’ll find 16.600, the highest day that still falls inside the whisker.
Change the filter to wind > 17.65: next to Minimum you’ll find 18.400, the lowest that falls outside.
Switch the filter off again afterwards — otherwise everything after this is computed on only a handful of days.



And this is how you check the two numbers from answer d) of Your turn: divide the difference between mean and median by the standard deviation of the same column, as Descriptives shows it.

wind: 0.16 / 3.575 = 0.045
ozone: 10.63 / 32.988 = 0.322





◠ Same shape in the book
Here: two middles pulling apart, and the heap that gives away why.
In the book: Chapter 2 — The Shape of the Heap
There you learn to read distributions before you summarise them — first the shape, then the number that may stand for the shape.
